The exceptions arise from five Directives that were adopted at the same time. They are the following, but each of these is a "Directive containing individual rights" (as they are referred to in the decision).
The 1976 right to respect for private and family life (under the guise of the right to information on state grounds for refusing consent to entry into the country)
The 1977 right to protection of property against State restrictions
The 1989 right to a social security system
The 1991 right to inspection of "administrative files" (of the authorities)
The 1993 equal pay Directive, which is not qualified by minimum terms at all.
In the first four cases, a violation by a citizen can be invoked before the court of a member state in a legal dispute with another citizen regarding, for example, a planned eviction, the sale of property, an administrative decision or a conflict about a child custody order. There, the court will look to the national law to see if it effectively implements the directive, and award damages if not. The effect here is mainly to encourage the application of human rights through member states' own laws. However, in none of these cases did the Court of Justice say that the individual could directly invoke the directive in court. Finally, any judicial review will be very limited in scope, focusing only on whether it is consistent with the order and with the minimum measures allowed by the directive. European law will not have taken over the area, and a national court would not act as a European court.
Only in respect to equal pay (but even only insofar as a national law is silent on a relevant issue), has the Court of Justice found standing to sue another individual, though only before national and then EU courts. The essence of this "oblique" effect was that the citizen may invoke an individual right as "conflicting with national law" in an application for an injunction to stop the infringement of the directive by the authority. If the court agrees, the national law will be struck down. Otherwise the State retains the right to apply that law. European law has been widely interpreted as a legal obstacle; if so, it replaces the conflicting national law and prevents any national government from applying it. However, no worker has ever been successful in this, and advocates complain of a "nebulous uncertainty" as a result of the exception.
On balance, the citizen does not have any "direct effect" of the majority of European Union law, but the "essential part" of the directive was given direct effect in the first four cases. Other "qualifying" directives (ones that contain "specific conditions") may also be given effect to the extent of those terms. Some EU law does give direct effect to citizens. For example, the Charter of Fundamental Rights can be invoked directly in EU law cases. EU citizenship confers certain rights and freedoms that EU law entitles an EU citizen to enjoy, however, that still depends on the disposition of member states. It has to be implemented by member states, and it remains subject to the permissiveness of the member state.

The Yuan dynasty further developed various traditional Chinese systems, such as the Jin shi examination system (with the policy of appointment based on merit adopted) and the Xuanzheng Yuan that formally incorporated Tibet into Chinese territory (the former Tibetans territories were defined as part of the area of the "Three Provinces of Tibet"). But the system of bureaucracy did not simply copy those of the Chinese dynasties. A particularly significant feature of the dynasty is the Mongol institution of Ulus (ulus) as it became the basic unit for government administration in many parts of the empire, such as the regions of Inner Mongolia, Rehe, Gansu and Turkestan, besides being the base for administration of the empire's subject peoples and nations. It consisted of an aggregation of Mongol clans, gers (yurts), associated by blood ties, economic interdependence and by the common allegiance to the khan and to the ruler of their respective Ulus. In terms of governance, the Ulus seems to have complemented, or even replaced, the traditional Chinese-style institutions at various times. 
In addition, there were also various other systems borrowed or copied from other cultures within the empire. The Jurchens' Department of Research and Narration was copied by the Yuan's Central Secretariat and the Liao dynasty's Southern Gates (殿前司) institution was copied to form the Privy Council. The Yuan government implemented a policy of regional ethnic separation and the conquered peoples within the empire were divided into different hierarchical categories for the purpose of managing the empire, which was influenced by Mongol and other Xianbei Turkish practices. The Khitan Liao Dynasty's governance of their empire, with its administrative division of China proper (including the Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun, Southern Yan, Southern Han, Wuyue, Northern Han, Northern Yan and the Liao Heartland) and the Non-Chinese Regions in the Northern Region, was also copied. Even the Tibetans' Buddhist institutions were adopted in the Yuan government in an attempt to integrate the highland peoples into the empire. It seems that in each conquered territory, the local forms of governance were adopted as long as they were not in conflict with the basic structure of Mongol governance. 
As the Empire expanded, most of the governmental agencies of the Yuan administration, including the Central Secretariat, the Censorate, the Privy Council, the Deliberative Assembly of Preeminent State Councilors (宰相會議), the Bureau of Judicial Review (肅政院), the Bureau of Military Affairs (尚軍所) and the Bureau of Imperial Clan Affairs (皇族內院), were established in the Yuan's capital Dadu. But some functions (such as administration of the military) and territories (such as the regions of Tibet, Sichuan, Yunnan, and some of Inner Mongolia) were transferred to the hands of officials in the provincial and local governments. Except for the provinces of Shaanxi and Sichuan that were directly governed by the Central Secretariat, the rest of the empire were governed by the Ten Circuits commissions (行中書省). The dual systems of circuit commissions and central agencies continued into the Ming dynasty.

The first vaccines were against smallpox and were introduced in the 18th century. Development of immunology began with the experiments of Louis Pasteur. Further landmark studies including the serological studies of Paul Ehrlich and the development of blood groups led to modern blood transfusion techniques. In 1900 it became clear from experiments of Paul Erlich that bacteria produce antigens specific to each species. This discovery led to the development of bacterial vaccines. Over the decades, improvements in vaccines and vaccination techniques led to dramatic drops in the morbidity and mortality due to infectious diseases.
The observation of a direct connection between infection with mumps virus and the development of Bell's palsy led to the conceptualization of pathogenesis, i.e., the process by which microbial infections lead to disease.

"Physical punishment" is a broad term referring to any punishment in which physical force is used and causes a painful or unpleasant sensation, including corporal punishment. It also includes less severe physical punishments that do not necessarily involve pain, such as hair-pulling, slapping without causing pain, or tapping. Psychological harm or the threat of physical punishment can also constitute physical punishment.

In legal contexts, the term "corporal punishment" is most often used to mean punishment that involves pain or physical damage. However, the precise definition varies. In some contexts it means any physical punishment, including needle punishments and punishments involving only a threat of physical contact. The most common usage, both in scholarship and in anti-spanking activism, defines it as punishment that involves "nonlethal" force that "is by design directly inflicted on the student's body." This definition is used, for example, by the United States National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), and by Amnesty International (AI).

Punishment by confinement, by being made to stand or sit for a period of time, by being denied food, warmth, exercise, or toilet facilities, and by being made to wear a rope衣 or stocks are all considered physical punishments, but are not considered corporal punishment. The same distinction applies to punishments that do not necessarily involve pain, such as hair-pulling, slapping without causing pain, or tapping. Psychological harm or the threat of physical punishment can also constitute physical punishment.

The harm caused by physical punishment does not always involve actual pain. The threat of physical pain is itself a harmful outcome, and this can constitute physical punishment. In some legal codes, physical punishment refers not only to those punishments that involve pain, but to any punishment that involves the use of force to which the person subjected to the punishment did not consent.
 
The concept of nonconsensual, physical punishment has long held a unique status. For example, the English judge wrote in 1889, "[I]t seems to me that the view that physical chastisement is a sort of duty resting on the owner of a child, whether the child will or not, is a view which common sense ought to condemn." However, nonconsensual physical punishment has historically been more widely accepted than other nonconsensual harm, such as assault.

<|math-wrapper|> The total number of ctenophores in the ocean is not known; it is estimated that there may be as many as 1 billion ctenophores in the ocean at any given time. Research has shown that ctenophores make up an average of around 5% of the marine zooplankton population, with most species having a population density between 1-30 individuals per cubic meter of water, although some have been recorded up to 3000 per cubic meter in certain conditions.
The diet of ctenophores consists mostly of protozoans, young crustaceans and the eggs of various marine species, including the polyps of various corals. Although many species of ctenophores are generalists, feeding on many different types of organisms, some are more specific in their prey selection. Ctenophore feeding involves capturing prey within sticky mucus entanglements on their tentacles, with the larger of the sticky mucus threads surrounded by colloblasts with a sticky glue-like substance. Once the prey is captured, it is passed towards the mouth through an “oral groove” formed by cilia moving along the tentacles. In the mouth, the food passes through a system of three internal canals, and is then distributed to eight cells within each combed body row. This is essentially the “digestive” system of the ctenophore.
<|endmath|> Ctenophores may breed year round, but the exact timings may vary, according to location. Many of these can reproduce sexually or asexually, either in the mature adults or during the larval stages of development. In asexual reproduction, the medusae reproduce through transverse fission, which is how juveniles form during early development. In sexual reproduction, eggs and sperm are released into the water, usually in a synchronized mating phase that takes place over a period of about two hours. The larvae, known as cydippid veligers, swim freely and are capable of feeding and growing in their early stages of life. It is believed that they develop into adults in about three weeks, although the exact timeline is still unknown.
Ctenophores can be found in a wide variety of marine environments. They are found in almost every ocean and sea, in both shallow and deep water, from the surface down to about 7,000 meters below. All ctenophores are free-swimming and can move through the water using their comb rows, which are grooves on their surfaces lined with specialized cells that produce a slimy substance when stimulated. These gelatinous organisms are either hermaphroditic or monoecious, and their reproductive strategies include both sexual and asexual reproduction. entities_raw:
In March 2013, Doctor Who: The Stolen Earth/The End of Time was released by Varese Sarabande as a two-disc set including music from the 2008, 2010 and 2011 specials (Planet of the Dead, The Stolen Earth, Army of Ghosts, Smith and Jones and The End of Time).
Doctor Who: The Eleventh Hour was released by Varese Sarabande in February 2014 in celebration of Matt Smith's two years in the role of the Eleventh Doctor. The album includes over 40 tracks from Smith's first two seasons including the soundtrack to "The Eleventh Hour" episode and the 50th anniversary specials.
In December 2014 the Doctor Who Original Television Soundtrack was released by La-La Land Recordings. This five-disc set featured tracks from season 4 to the present (The Next Doctor to Hell Bent).
In February 2017 a three-disc set was released which contained music from all of the various episodes (The Girl Who Dared to Dream and Let's Kill Hitler to The Dance Debacle). The soundtrack contained also a The Amazing Stories album, a bonus CD with SFX Radio recordings from RTÉ (Republic of Ireland) from 1984 to 1998.
In March 2017, five special edition soundtracks were announced and then released later in the month. "The 12th Doctor" soundtrack was released on 11 March with tracks from the last half of season 10. In April 2017, a three-disc set was released that contained music from the six part The Continuing Adventure of the Doctor series of short stories. In June 2017, Doctor Who: The 50th Anniversary Soundtrack was released on two discs. This included music from the Diamond Head featuring the TARDIS reconstructed scene, Time of the Doctor, Dark Water and Death in Heaven, The Day of the Doctor, The Time of the Doctor, Twice Upon a Time and The Final Days of the Doctor. In October 2017, a two-disc set was released which featured music from the stories "An Act of War", "Welcome to the Jungle", "The Lie of the Land", and "Extremis". In November 2017, the soundtrack "The Other Worlds" was released containing music from the following stories: "Hell Bent", "Cradle of Fear", "Journey to the Centre of Earth", "Citadel of Mist", "Alien Bodies", "The Day of the Doctor" and "Hell Bent". In December 2017, a special edition four disc set, including the original soundtracks, was released. It also contains bloopers, outtakes, main cast/crew interviews and Q&A with the composer, Dominic Glynn, and Claire Treadwell, Sound Design Coordinator, on "The Snowmen". In May 2018 the soundtrack "The Master - The First of The Time Lords" was released, including tracks from the adventures "The Woman Who Lived", "The Witch's Familiar" and "Autosensorial Sensory Deprivation". In July 2018, two special edition four disc soundtracks were released, "The Master of Nerva" and "The End of Time" that both included the original soundtracks, bloopers, outtakes, main cast/crew interviews and Q&A with the composer, Dominic Glynn, and Claire Treadwell, Sound Design Coordinator, for the "Dark Water" and "Death in Heaven" and "The Next Doctor" and "The Time of the Doctor" adventures respectively. In August 2018, the Soundtrack Doctor Who Complete Box set was released that included all seven soundtrack albums to the series released since 2010. In November 2018, the Doctor Who First Series Classic Soundtrack album was released, featuring music from all episodes from the first series of the programme. In May 2019, Doctor Who The 51st Anniversary Soundtrack was released with tracks from The Day of the Doctor and Twice Upon a Time. In July 2019 Doctor Who: Mission to Bavaris was released, containing bloopers, outtakes, main cast/crew interviews and Q&A with the composer, Dominic Glynn, for the "Mission to Bavaris" story.

What is the result of the sum $\frac{1}{5} + \frac{2}{5} + \frac{3}{5} + \dots + \frac{9}{5} + \frac{10}{5}$?
The sum in question is the sum of the fractions \(\frac{1}{5} + \frac{2}{5} + \frac{3}{5} + \dots + \frac{9}{5} + \frac{10}{5}\). We can factor out the common denominator of 5 from each term, which simplifies the sum to:

\[
\frac{1}{5} + \frac{2}{5} + \frac{3}{5} + \dots + \frac{9}{5} + \frac{10}{5} = \frac{1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + 9 + 10}{5}
\]

The numerator is the sum of the first 10 positive integers. The sum of the first \(n\) positive integers is given by the formula:

\[
\frac{n(n+1)}{2}
\]

In this case, \(n = 10\), so we have:

\[
1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + 10 = \frac{10 \cdot 11}{2} = 55
\]

Now, we substitute this back into our fraction:

\[
\frac{1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + 9 + 10}{5} = \frac{55}{5} = 11
\]

Therefore, the result of the sum is:

\[
\boxed{11}
\]

To find all positive integers \( n \) satisfying \( s(n) \mid n \) and \( s(n+2014) = s(n) \), we start by analyzing the given conditions.

First, let's consider the condition \( s(n+2014) = s(n) \). This implies that the sum of the digits of \( n \) is the same as the sum of the digits of \( n + 2014 \). Developers should ensure that their tools are trained on diverse and representative data sets, and regularly monitor and evaluate the impact of their tools on different user groups.

4. Consent and Control: Users should have the right to consent to and control the use of their data, including the ability to access and delete their data when they wish. Developers should provide users with clear information about how their data will be used, and ensure that they have the ability to control their data preferences and settings.

5. Responsible Innovation: Developers should consider the potential impact of their tools on society, including the potential for harm or unintended consequences. They should prioritize responsible innovation, conducting ethical reviews of their tools and actively seeking feedback from experts, stakeholders, and the public throughout the development process.

To ensure that digital communication tools enhance human-AI collaboration rather than hinder it, developers should also consider the following:

1. User-Centered Design: Tools should be designed with the needs and goals of users in mind. This involves conducting user research, incorporating user feedback into the design process, and testing the tools with a diverse set of users to ensure they are accessible and effective.

2. Support for Collaboration: Tools should facilitate effective communication and collaboration between human and AI experts, allowing them to work together seamlessly and efficiently. This may involve features such as real-time collaboration, automatic translation, and seamless data integration.

3. Promoting Trust and Confidence: Developers should work to build trust and confidence in their tools, by providing clear explanations of how they work, demonstrating their effectiveness through case studies and research, and engaging in ongoing dialogue with users and experts.

    # Return the entity count dictionary
    return entity_count_dict

Inserting text into a table based on a certain category using SQL involves several steps. Let's assume you have a table named `products` with columns `product_id`, `category`, and `description`. You want to insert a new row into the table where the `category` matches a specific value, say 'electronics'.

Here's how you can achieve this:

1. **Check if the category exists:**
   Before inserting a new row, it's good practice to check if the category already exists in the table. This prevents any errors and ensures that the data is accurate.
   
   ```sql
   SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products WHERE category = 'electronics';
   ```

2. **Insert the new row:**
   If the category exists, you can proceed to insert the new row. Otherwise, you may need to handle the case where the category doesn't exist, depending on your requirements.

   ```sql
   -- Assuming the category exists
   INSERT INTO products (product_id, category, description)
   VALUES (10001, 'electronics', 'Description for the electronic product');
   ```

3. **Updating existing records:**
   If you want to update an existing record instead of inserting a new one, you can use an `UPDATE` statement:

   ```sql
   UPDATE products
   SET description = 'Updated description for the electronic product'
   WHERE product_id = 10001 AND category = 'electronics';
   ```

4. **Using a CASE statement (if necessary):**
   If you have multiple categories to handle and want to insert text into a table based on a certain category, you can use a `CASE` statement within your `INSERT` or `UPDATE` query. -- Insert the new customer

Now we will examine the definition of some complexity classes in greater detail.
### Computational complexity theory
Computational complexity theory is a branch of the theory of computation in theoretical computer science that focuses on classifying computational problems according to their inherent difficulty, and relating those classes to each other. A computational problem is understood to be a task that is in principle amenable to being solved by a computer, which is equivalent to stating that the problem may be solved by mechanical application of mathematical steps, such as an algorithm.

A problem is regarded as inherently difficult if its solution requires significant resources, whatever the algorithm used. The theory formalizes this intuition, by introducing mathematical models of computation to study these problems and quantifying the amount of resources needed to solve them, such as time and storage. Other complexity measures are also used, such as the amount of communication (used in communication complexity), the number of gate Delays (used in circuit complexity), and the number of processors (used in parallel computing).

# Complexity classes
### Complexity classes in terms of the Turing machine
The standard model to study the time complexity of a problem is the deterministic Turing machine which consists of a Read head, an infinitely long tape with read/write access to each cell, and a deterministic finite state machine that governs the action of the machine for each state/tape combination. The machine starts from the leftmost symbol of the input on a blank tape (saturated with blank symbols). It then proceeds through a set of transitions in its internal state based on its current state and the symbol it has just read from the tape, and follows some algorithm of computation in order to solve the problem. The time required to solve a problem X by a Turing machine M is the number of transitions/operations made by the Turing machine M before solving X. Usually, the time complexity of a Turing machine M that solves a problem X is written as T_M(X). Thus, T_M(X) = t for a given input X if the Turing machine M solves X in t steps and t is the least among all Turing machines that solve X. Formally, the time complexity of a Turing machine M solving a problem X is
T_M(X)=min\{t:M solves X in t steps\}
The time complexity of a problem X is then the minimum time needed to solve X by a Turing machine. The time complexity of a problem is therefore the minimum time needed by any Turing machine that solves X. Since there is a trivial Turing machine that simply does not perform any operation, the time complexity of a problem X is usually defined to be at least one.
### Complexity classes in terms of the RAM machine
The other standard model of computation is the Random Access Machine (RAM). Unlike the Turing machine model, the RAM model assumes that basic operations such as incrementing a counter takes one step. Thus, the RAM machine is closer to a real computer than the Turing machine is. This model is easier to reason about, since one does not have to keep track of the number of steps. Also, since the RAM model assumes that basic operations such as incrementing a counter take one step, the time complexity is usually an accurate estimate of the number of basic operations to be performed, whereas in the Turing machine model, the time complexity is only an upper bound of the number of basic operations to be performed.
### Complexity classes in terms of the PRAM
A PRAM (Parallel Random Access Machine) is a theoretical Parallel Computer Model. It is closely related to the RAM model except that PRAM models allow several processors to read and write on the same memory without encountering conflicts. PRAM models thus are a good way of formally describing a parallel computer. PRAM is a multi-tape Turing machine with multiple heads. It has unbounded memory and word size where all memory cells are connected to the processor so that each processor can read from and write to any cell. A parallel algorithm is said to be efficient if it runs in polylogarithmic time in the size of the input n. In order to avoid conflicts in the writing operations, some PRAM machine models also include synchronization instructions.
### Complexity classes in terms of the Skew Heap
The Skew Heap is a self-adjusting binary heap data structure. The operations on a skew heap are similar to those on a binary heap. The operations that the skew heap provides include Insertion and Deletion. The key difference between the skew heap and the binary heap is that it does not perform a balancing operation, instead it uses only structure maintaining operations. A skew heap consists of a collection of binary heaps where each binary heap is a subtree rooted at the binary heap. It can be implemented using a binary tree where each node has two children and one parent, other than the root node.
### Complexity classes in terms of the Hash table
A hash table is a data structure that uses hashing to associate keys with values. A hash table supports four main operations: insert, delete, search, and key lookup. All these operations can be performed in O(1) time. Hashing is a simple way to store and look up data in a large dataset. To implement hashing, one must define a hash function that maps keys to integers. The integer that results from applying this function is then used as an index into a table of fixed length to access the value. The key is simply the index into this table. The hash function must be chosen carefully, in order to avoid collisions between different values.

BPP, ZPP and RP are defined using probabilistic Turing machines. These entities represent different realms of computational problems, each defined by the probabilistic characteristics of its associated Turing machine. BPP machines are probabilistic machines with a bounded probability of error, ZPP machines are machines that require only polylogarithmic space and no time, and RP machines are probabilistic machines that provide a correct answer most of the time. The intersections between these entities offer unique insights into the behavior of randomized algorithms in terms of efficiency and correctness.

### AC and NC
AC and NC are defined using Boolean circuits. These classes represent parallel computational problems, where the complexity is measured by the depth and size of the circuits that solve them. AC captures problems that can be solved efficiently in parallel, while NC captures problems that can be solved efficiently in parallel and are deterministic. The relationship between these entities reveals the influence of parallelism on computational efficiency and the power of boolean circuits in solving complex problems.

### BQP and QMA
BQP and QMA are defined using quantum Turing machines. BQP represents the class of problems that can be efficiently solved on a quantum computer, while QMA is the quantum analog of the classical complexity class NP. The interaction between these entities highlights the potential of quantum computing in tackling problems that are intractable for classical computers, such as factoring and certain search problems.

### #P
#P is a complexity class that deals with counting problems. Unlike decision problems, which only involve "yes" or "no" answers, counting problems involve counting the number of solutions to a given problem. The relationship between #P and other complexity classes sheds light on the inherent difficulty of counting problems and the challenges associated with solving them efficiently.

### Interaction between BPP, ZPP and RP and AC, NC, BQP, QMA, #P

The connection between these entities further demonstrates the rich tapestry of computational complexity theory, where different types of machines and algorithms coexist and interact in intricate ways. Suppose every male who prefers tea has an additional sibling. If 30% of the males are bilingual and 20% of the bilingual males prefer tea, how many males are there in total?
To solve this problem, let's break it down into manageable steps. We'll start by setting up the relationships given in the problem and then use these relationships to derive the total number of males.

1. Let \( T \) be the number of males who prefer tea.
2. Since every male who prefers tea has an additional sibling, the number of additional siblings is equal to \( T \). So, the total number of siblings is \( T \).
3. Let \( B \) be the number of bilingual males. Since 30% of the males are bilingual, the number of bilingual males is \( B = 0.3M \), where \( M \) is the total number of males.
4. Let \( T_B \) be the number of bilingual males who prefer tea. Since 20% of the bilingual males prefer tea, the number of bilingual males who prefer tea is \( T_B = 0.2B = 0.2 \times 0.3M = 0.06M \).
5. Since every male who prefers tea has an additional sibling, the number of additional siblings is equal to \( T \). Since all bilingual males who prefer tea are included in this number, \( T \geq 0.06M \). But we don't need to use this directly here, we just need to use the fact that the number of males who prefer tea is the same as the number of additional siblings, which is \( T \).

Since we don't have a specific value for \( T \), we can express the total number of males \( M \) in terms of \( T \). From the fact that \( T = T_B \), we have \( T = 0.06M \). Rearranging this, we get \( M = \frac{T}{0.06} = \frac{25T}{3} \).

So, the total number of males \( M \) is \( \frac{25T}{3} \). To find a specific numerical answer, we need the value of \( T \). However, since we don't have that information, we can assume \( T \) is a value that makes \( M \) an integer. Let's assume \( T = 3 \), then \( M = \frac{25 \times 3}{3} = 25 \).

Let's verify the logic with Python code. We'll assume \( T = 3 \) and check the consistency of the solution.

The following year, 1754, the French sent a larger force to the Ohio Country under Claude-Pierre Pécaudy de Contrecœur to aid Marin. Contrecœur led a force south from Fort Niagara and established Fort Venango (near modern Franklin, Pennsylvania) on July 31, 1754. From Fort Venango, he sent a scouting party of thirty French and several hundred Indians south. They traveled up the Allegheny River before following a trail to the Nemacolin Path. On May 28, they arrived at the Great Meadows and pitched camp. The camp was discovered by local chief Tanaghrisson, who agreed to help the French build a bridge. When word of Tanaghrisson's alliance with the French reached the colonial government in Virginia, Governor Robert Dinwiddie sent more than 50 British troops with Tanaghrisson and a party of Mingo to demand that the French leave the area. When the British presence was discovered by the French, they sent a patrol of twenty French regulars, several Indians, and two soldiers under the command of Joseph Coulon de Villiers de Jumonville. Their goal was to secure a land grant for a future settlement, strategically located at the forks of the Ohio River. The French were likely unaware of the change in local alliances, and ignored Tanaghrisson and his party. When Jumonville's patrol was attacked by colonial militiamen, Tanaghrisson beheaded and scalped Jumonville, exclaiming "The Great Spirit will avenge the death of Jumonville." The resulting incident became known as the Fright of Jumonville Glen. It was the opening battle of the French and Indian War, which began four years earlier in the European theater as King George's War, and continued on a larger scale until 1763. British violence against and deportations of Native Americans (along with French allied Europeans and Native Americans) within the Ohio Country pushed them towards French alliance. Tanaghrisson and the Mingo allied with the Virginia militia as chief allies in 1755 as well as in other militia and regular forces under several colonial governments and under British regulars. Later, American historian Francis Parkman, gave Tanaghrisson the nickname the "Sauvage General" (The Seats of the Conquerors).
As 1754 continued, the British decided to build a road through the Great Meadows and construct a fort at the headwaters of the two branches of the Forbes Trail that ran south from Fort Venango. Tanaghrisson and his Mingo allies once again attacked Native American villages allied with the French. This time, they struck at the village of Chigachgog (present-day Kittanning, Pennsylvania) on August 29, massacring several dozen men, women and children. In the following weeks, Tanaghrisson's forces traveled south to attack French positions. While they were unsuccessful at Fort Saint-Pierre, they did plunder and destroy Fort Duquesne (present-day Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) on September 10. The destruction and pillaging of Fort Duquesne was witnessed by Pennsylvania's colonial governor, William Shirley. Shocked by the destruction wrought by Tanaghrisson and his allies, Shirley immediately ordered the construction of a new fort, the much smaller Fort Cumberland (near present-day Cumberland, Maryland) to serve as a new path through the Cumberland Valley. During winter of 1754 and early spring, Tanaghrisson visited Fort Cumberland and was fed by the British colonists. Although this likely failed to dampen any Mingo hostility towards the British, it did temporarily alleviate them from hostilities.[3]
Beginning in 1756, British colonial militiamen continued their deadly campaigns against Native Americans, and numerous militia officers ordered villages on the order of execution. The attacks against local villages from Kittanning to Ohio and beyond sparked a fierce response. Native American warriors allied with both French and British attacked British settlers and the Fort Cumberland garrison. Responding to Mingo destruction of the new settlement at Dickinson's Folly (also known as Draper's Meadows, on the Ohio River south of what is now Richeyville, West Virginia), British colonists under Commander George Washington and Colonel Joshua Fry deployed their troops against the town of Chigachgog. The expedition left Fort Cumberland on June 13, 1756 and arrived at the western-most British outpost of Fort New Waterford (present-day Waterford, Pennsylvania) on June 24. The army spent the night at Fort New Waterford and set up camp the next day. The next morning, July 3, 1756, Washington ordered the camp struck and the soldiers to march southeast to Chigachgog. The British army soon discovered Indians camped nearby. They attacked the Indian camp and burned houses that were in the village.
Earlier that same day, Indian warriors who had been found living in the Chigachgog village discovered the approaching British forces. After observing the British troops leave their base camp near Fort New Waterford, the warriors rode back to the village. The warriors then lit a signal fire and released a number of blackbirds, which had been held captive. They had learned that in Mingo tradition, this was a signal for all warriors to flee. The British followed the fleeing warriors, but did not pursue them once they discovered the village was deserted. They set fire to the village and destroyed most of the warriors' possessions. #### Eva Hesse. Estate of Eva Hesse/BFAC, NY. Photograph: Malin Theodore

Eva Hesse (1936–70) experimented with various media but is best known for her sculptural works, which, with her heroic posthumous reputation, stand at the forefront of postwar American art. Hesse struggled between clinical detachment and expressive energy, between the handmade and the machine made, between labor-intensive yet never finished forms and the concise definition of materiality. In this fine, semi-abstract work, the knobbly, weathered look of the unplastered wall is on one level the stuff of sculpture, but it also recalls the time-worn, time-stunted head of an old crone, voodoo doll, devil woman or witch. The crude presence of this "performative" sculpture is a defiant assertion of its very materiality. Its stylistic language seems archaic, yet its function as sculpture is self-possessed.

Enclosed in a simple, shallow wooden box that resembles a recipe book or travel guide, the sculpture owes a debt to the kind of functional box with which it shares its title and to the postwar appetite for the international style. The inner surface of this box is lined with an acid yellow paper bearing the word "WIDE" in smudgy typographic smears. This paper, contrasting brightly with the dark brown wooden box, is accented by at least two kinds of letters—blue or yellow stripes are streaked on some of the boxes, others are painted with the word "Web" in neat yellow and blue lines. While these words are printed and painted haphazardly, the work as a whole is tidy and clean. Without any attempt at concealment, its paper is exposed, its innermost, structural box holds things in suspense, and its materials are shown openly. Over the 1970s and ‘80s Niki de Saint Phalle sought to reach the widest possible public for her large-scale installations, sculptures, public art, and events. “Open air” (air libre), as she liked to call it, involved the use of enormous architectural-scale sculpture outdoors, frequently in collaboration with architects, but often outside architecture. She was especially interested in spaces (such as airports) where she would be an unexpected element. Arguably, the basic elements of “open air” as deployed by Saint Phalle could be expressed in the form of a triangle: huge, bright, hand-painted, three-dimensional figures juxtaposed with the (usually) flat gray of the environment, in which figures are engaged in non-human activities of all kinds—running, fighting, playing, flying, spinning, seeing—usually on black steel metal plates. These minimalist plates became part of a long-term, media-rich spectacle of performance, observing, listening, gawking, and taking photographs.

Materiality and the expressions of a human presence are fundamental, as their principle is direct contact and viewership with a public sculpture. Thus, “open air” is a form of museum as such. It might be said, “open air” is a museum which focuses on the public, engages multiple possible aesthetic and referential spheres simultaneously, and is activated as much by verbal translation (by exhibition materials) and a sense of play, chance, and surprise as by its material presence. This is not meant to detract from the sculptural value of Saint Phalle’s sculptures, as both their continuity and discontinuity or both their planar surface and their interiority establish their very complex material presence.

The museum closed from March until July 2001, and again from 2008 to 2012, for a redevelopment programme which created three storeys of new gallery space and better access to the museum. Two other buildings, both opened in 1999, contain offices and additional gallery space.
 The museum was originally established in 1852 at Marlborough House as the Manufacturing Society's Museum, which came under the control of the Society for the Encouragement of National Industry (SENI), a government-sponsored "industrial and fine arts" organization. The museum was transferred to the control of the Commissioners of Her Majesty's Works in the Autumn of 1852. It was renamed the Museum of Manufactures, and by December, had been moved to Somerset House, with a collection of decorative arts and paintings from the King's Gallery. Four other locations in London were considered before the museum finally settled in a building on the site of Brompton Park House in South Kensington in 1854, by which time its name had been changed to the South Kensington Museum. Queen Victoria and Prince Albert held a royal sale of artworks in December 1855, which was moved to the museum in January 1856. The Royal Academy threatened to withdraw their annual summer exhibition if it was held in the museum as it considered the museum to be "dirty and disreputable"; as a result, the museum was closed in 1857. Prince Albert interfered to have the museum opened on schedule. Prince Albert also sold part of the royal art collection to the museum; the return on this transaction was sold in 1858 to pay for the rental of the building. On 25 June 1856, Queen Victoria agreed in principle to finance a new building for the museum in her private estate; however, she withdrew the offer in favour of the earl of Highgate's Merton Estate at the Royal Horticultural Society's request. This led Prince Albert and Lionel de Rothschild, president of the SENI, to seek Parliament's support, which resulted in the 1856 Victoria and Albert Museum Act, in which the SENI was reconstituted as the V&A. The museum was re-opened in Somerset House in April 1857 as the Science and Art Museum, which consisted of science and industry displays alongside the existing fine arts collections. The museum was again relocated when its new premises opened in 1885, with the last sections of the museum being divided between the south and north wings. Richard Redgrave was appointed keeper at the Victoria and Albert Museum in 1861, taking over from Henry Cole, the first keeper of the museum, who had resigned after losing a four-year salary dispute with the SENI. The Victoria and Albert Museum was granted its current charter by Queen Victoria in 1909. After Redgrave resigned in 1886, Henry Cole was reinstated as the keeper of the museum in 1892 for the second time. Henry Cole retired in 1893, and William Frend Wroughton took over as the new keeper of the museum, which closed in 1909 to allow a complete reorganisation. In 1889 the museum's collections of stained glass were transferred to the new British Museum of Ornamental Art, which was renamed the Bargello Museum in 1897, due to confusion with the older British Museum. The collection was transferred to the Victoria and Albert Museum in 1900.
The museum began to be widely used by the public in 1888, after the architects Aston Webb and Samuelmenu> Hardwicke appointed at the museum designed the South Kensington Museum extension. A three-year project began in 1901 to prepare the building for the celebrations of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee; galleries for Japanese art, carpets, and tapestries were opened, and the Great Hall, which was home to the museum's sculpture collection, was completed and opened to the public in 1902. The museum closed for a reorganisation in 1909, including a complete redesign of the museum, which opened to the public in 1913. The redevelopment included the refurbishment of the garden and the construction of a new northern entrance, designed by Sir Aston Webb, with two towers representing Greece and Italy. It was later (1919–24) enlarged again by Charles Holden. Following the 1913 reorganisation, the museum's collection expanded rapidly, and the building began to feel cramped; as a result, the first phase of the South Kensington Museum Extension was opened in 1929, with the renovation and enlargement of the Edward VII memorial gardens (which became the Treacock, Reynolds, and Boulton Foundations gardens) which was completed by Gertrude Jekyll and John Nash in 1930. The site was still too small, and a later redesign of the museum included a plan to build a new wing on the north side of Victoria Gardens; this was abandoned in 1934. The construction of a new department of decorative arts was made possible by the founding of the John Madejski Foundation in 1973, and after the death of chairman Charlie Havighurst, who had founded the foundation, the John Madejski Garden was opened in 2008. During the redevelopment, a new space for exhibitions opened in 2009, before the section of the museum devoted to silversmithing was closed in 2010. New installation spaces were created in 2012 to promote the use of new technologies, including exhibitions which use both augmented reality and mobile apps to connect with objects in the museum. A new theatre, designed by theatre architect David Mackie, opened in 2012.

Private schools, for most of the period of apartheid, were completely segregated.
Students who were white, coloured or Indian had separate independent schools, while students who were black went to government schools. After the abolition of apartheid, the laws governing private education changed significantly.
The South African Schools Act of 1996 recognises two categories of schools: "public" (state-controlled) and "independent" (which includes traditional private schools and schools which are privately governed[clarification needed].)

There is no mention of a special category for traditional private schools as was the case under apartheid.
But although it is now "legal" for independent schools to admit black students and other groups which were excluded during apartheid, most (if not all) independent schools are virtually all-white, and make no great effort to attract black students.

## Private schools in South Africa
Before the apartheid era, under British rule, very few black children received any formal education.
Most of these children attended small government schools run by local catechists, who also became the initial teachers at Mission schools when these were established.
The first privately funded schools run by missionaries were established in 1820 in Natal and 1824 in the Cape Colony.
Very few black students were admitted to these schools during the early decades of the nineteenth century because such a small number of the population of colour were literate.

Overall, the complexity class P plays a crucial role in understanding the computational efficiency of various problems. It provides a basis for comparing the performance of algorithms and determining the feasibility of solving different types of problems within a given amount of time.

The Peasants' War, also known as the Great Peasants' War or German Peasants' War (German: Deutsch-Bauernkrieg), was a popular revolt in many of the German-speaking states of the Holy Roman Empire against their rulers, combining social revolution in the rural areas with an attempt by the Protestant Reformation to change the structure of the Empire. It came to a climax in 1525 with the Battle of Frankenhausen, in which most of the rebels were defeated. Later uprisings included the Münster Rebellion of 1534–35, a prominent example of Anabaptism.

Historical background
Events that led to the rebellion began in 1495 with the enactment of the Bold Charter by the Elector of Saxony. This document promised to redistribute land among the people and reduce the expenses of the peasants. However, it was never put into effect.
Two years later, the so-called Basel Compacts were made with the purpose of reducing the expenses of the peasants. These three compacts, called the Peace of Welschbillig, the Peace of St. Leziers, and the Pforzheimer Conventions, attempted to reduce, with long-term plans, the expenses of the peasants. However, none of them was ever implemented by the rulers.
The regime of Charles V
In 1522 and 1523, the town of Augsburg made two plans for reform and alleviation of the burdens on the peasantry. Though the plans were discussed with the council of Augsburg, they were never put into effect. By that time, the Reformation had been underway for seven years. In the Free City of Nuremberg, the town council, under Hans Gösser, instructed its priests to enforce what the council perceived as an accurate and loyal interpretation of the Gospel; the council attempted to reduce both the income and the influence of the local bishop.
The first directives of the Reformation
The first directives, known as the Twelve Articles of the German Peasants' War, were authored in Wittenberg at the request of local and regional preachers and published in August 1525 in the form of pamphlets in most of the towns in southern Germany. Their authorship is accredited to Andreas Pollanka, a carpenter's apprentice from Augsburg. It's speculated that the leading figure of the revolt, Thomas Müntzer, could have had a hand in their composition as well. The Twelve Articles united the concerns of both peasants and local bourgeoisie. The document itself addressed over a dozen grievances including obligations to the lords, compulsory services, and farm animals.
The outbreak of the revolt
In May 1524, the Pilgrimage War (German: Pilgerkrieg), an armed conflict against the rulers and retainers of the Holy Roman Empire was declared by peasant groups in western Germany. This was primarily a response to the war waged by Charles V against the Lutherans in the 1523-25 Reichsdeichsganze, in which the Lutherans had gained a tremendous number of both political allies and ecclesiastical privileges.
While the fighting in western Germany continued, in Bavaria the revolt was re-ignited by unrest among the peasants, and the leading figure of this new phase of the conflict was Thomas Müntzer. Under Müntzer's leadership, a confession (German: Schwertbrief or sword-epistle) was drafted, declaring, among other things, that none were free except the preachers and rebels. As the leader of the movement, Müntzer received a number of delegations of the Swabian peasants. Meanwhile, a number of governments also sent their envoys to meet with Müntzer to convince him to abandon the revolt. Müntzer was persistent in his determinations, while his adherents quickly grew in numbers.
Heberhagen reports in the Erlanger Nachrichten that there had been a big number of rebellions and raids. The Districts of Kurpfalz and Altmühltal, the Wirtzgau north of Schwabien, the Pottelsbach and the Upper Main valley had a few others, besides the Wetterau area and Thuringia. Bavaria and Frising also saw some, while in the Swabian Forest and the Ulm area, the Frising area and the Stromberg, rebels held out against the allies of the authorities of Württemberg. Those in Bavaria and the district of Württemberg declared that they would fight only against "the army of knights and nobles" and would only accept "saintly law", and would ultimately be guided by the direction of the preachers. The "Instructions of St. Matthew" is reported to have been circulated throughout the land and used as a guide by the forces of resistance, when the servants of the clergy were told to hand over their mallets and censers and take up swords.
Early successes and the Kappel peasants' union
At the beginning of July, a Zürich priest by the name of Balthasar Hubmaier made an appeal to the troops of the armies, instructing them that it was a sin to commit atrocities against women and children. On 11 July, a Bavarian council from Landshut gave the peasants an ultimatum to end the "resistance" and "disobedience" or face attacks from troops commanded by the Emperor Maximilian's brother, Philip the Handsome, Duke of Burgundy. The council also put out a warning to the local nobility to withdraw their support of the rebels, or be regarded as aggressors by the troops of Philip.
When the "rebellious peasants" declared that they wouldn't do so, Philip assembled an army led by the conservative Anabaptist Preacher Ludwig Haetzer of Munich on 22 July. The group, made up of an army of between 13,000 and 15,000 men, then marched west. The Bavarian council on 22 July authorised the formation of a peasant contingent to resist the troops, and on 26 July a military leader was named, who was afterwards known as Baron Ziezemer (Thomas Ziehos), and was chosen as the leader by the peasants.
On 28 July, the United Bavarian Confederation elected a 14-member delegation to negotiate with Philip. The delegates included a local Anabaptist preacher from Miesbach, named Jacob Weidmann, who two days later was also sent to the Anabaptists that had taken refuge in the Wartburg to see if they were interested in negotiating.
On 1 August, the Anabaptists, led by Thomas Müntzer, agreed to negotiate a truce with the authorities, that included the surrendering of the fortifications taken over by the rebels. But before the attackers could comply, the Duke of Burgundy made a surprise attack in Neuhaus, that left the rebel army leaderless and unable to turn to the Wartburg.
On the same day, the council of Erlangen issued an ultimatum to the rebels, which they ignored and two days later Philip and his troops started to march east toward Nuremberg, where Müntzer and his followers now were holding out. In order to defend the city, the authorities mobilised some 4,000 militiamen. There were disputes among the leaders of the revolt, and so the troops didn't agree to continue fighting the Duke, who was now passing by Nuremberg. On 30 August, the Bavarian contingent finally reached Nuremberg, and two days later the Duke of Burgundy had left.
The rebels were now led by Ziehos, who on 2 September organised a camp at the New City Gate. At about the same time, a delegation from the Freiburg Council arrived with the request that the rebels should be allowed to leave. The request was rejected by Ziehos, who ordered his troops to fight. The leaders of the uprising were from the beginning made clear that they would not give up arms for anything or anyone, but had decided to "fight, drink and die".
The end of the revolt
In September 1525, the troops of the divided alliance commanded by the Electors of Saxony and Brandenburg-Meissen, Duke Ulrich of Württemberg, and the city-state of Strasbourg marched into Württemberg. The Austrians and the troops led by the Electors took the Swabian Forest region, and Ulrich marched into the region of the Breisgau. After Ulrich had crossed the river Upper Rhine, he reported to Döfflingen, the seat of the chapter house of the Breisgau, that the territory was clearly free of the "enemy troops", but as he entered, the chapter refused to surrender its valley fortress. Eventually, the city sent a large military force and made the mission to take the fortress impossible, which ended in Ulrich having to flee the area.
In the area around Schwabach and Braunau, the local mercenaries had rebelled against their commander and moved toward Nuremberg. The Nuremberg troops decided to stop them at Frankenhausen, where a revolt had begun. On 15 May 1525, the troops of Ulrich had caught up with them. Thirty minutes after the battle started, the rebels had retreated.
The rebellion was now almost completely suppressed, and the separatist forces were no longer in a position to wage war, and were defeated by smaller military forces that the ruling classes had gathered. The concept of packet switching had already been developed by Leonard Kleinrock during his PhD studies. However, unlike Baran's work on a completely distributed network, Kleinrock was developing an alternative scheme, the cell relay.

Packet switching network
A packet switching network is a network of interconnected nodes. The nodes on the network route packets of data to their destination node.
In packet switching, packets are routed individually. In contrast, circuit switching carries one complete conversation or session over a dedicated connection from start to end. A connection must be created at the start of a packet exchange and torn down at the end. In packet switching, the transmitting node does not need to reserve bandwidth in advance. It simply waits until the network has sufficient capacity.
The three phases of packet switching: pack, route, and deliver.
Since the routing is performed on a per-packet basis, it is not necessary to ensure that the nodes on the network are synchronized (unlike in circuit switching). The routing of packets is easier than that in circuit switching because no setup phase is required. The amount of processing for routing an individual packet is usually the same in both methods, but this is done frequently in packet switching, because each packet must be routed individually.
Packet switching can either be virtual circuit or datagram. The first type creates permanent connections between two nodes or groups of nodes, which is similar to circuit switching, and the second type creates temporary connections between two nodes or groups of nodes for as long as needed.
Advantages and disadvantages of packet switching
Examples of packet switching networks are X.25, Frame Relay, Ethernet, Wi-Fi, and Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM). Packet switching uses data packets, but the protocol to create connections and exchange messages is different from the communication used by the internet (TCP/IP). Nevertheless, packet switching is often seen as the predecessor to internet technologies. Examples of packet switching networks that support TCP/IP are Ethernet and Wi-Fi.

Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) is a mature packet switching technology that has been widely deployed in the past for high-speed internet networks to provide connection-oriented transport. It was built to leverage the capabilities of optical transport technologies of the time. Its development was largely driven by telecommunications carriers who saw the need for a digital equivalent of their circuit switching networks for data communications. ATM was an evolution of the principles behind packet switching. The technology's adoption was limited due to the advent of scalable solutions such as Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS), which was less complex to manage for end users. ATM is now rarely used for general data communications, but is commonly used as a packet switching backplane within computer switches and routers.

Baran's 1962 description
In this paragraph, the roles of the transmitter, receiver, and third party nodes are clarified.

The transmitter is actually composed of one or more transmitting devices (terminals) connected to the "input lines" of the communications network. Each transmitting device is assigned a unique identity in the communications network.
The receiver is composed of one or more receiving devices (terminals) connected to the "output lines" of the communications network. Each receiving device is also assigned a unique identity in the communications network.
Each receiving device also has a transmitting device with which it has established a communications session.
Each transmitting device has a receiving device with which it has established a communications session. This receiving device may or may not be the same as the transmitting device to which it is directly connected.
In practice, the systems will have many more terminal connections than the number of links shown in figure 1.
The intermediate nodes in the communications network are called third party nodes. Every intermediate node of the communications network has at least one input line and one output line, but can have any number of lines. The location of these nodes is flexible.
In reality, many communications networks require only a limited number of two-party nodes to be added for internal connections. Many of these nodes are called "circulation points" in Baran's paper. These circulation points are devices that use multiple links to a number of third party nodes to transmit data between two third party nodes.
This arrangement is used because it is usually more economical to establish an intermediate node at one point in a communications network than at both ends of a connection. In this way, each intermediate node can share the cost of creating a connection between any two third party nodes within the communications network. Most nodes do not require the full processing power of a two-party node and can be satisfied by limited software and a smaller physical location.
Modern communications networks use fully integrated optical cross-connects for inter-office switching between service-provider networks. They could be used instead of multiple point-to-point communication circuits for each node, or each node could use a limited processing node for a complete inter-node communications network for cheaper point-to-point connections.
The third party nodes (intermediate nodes) receive packets, analyze them, and rewrite them, and pass them on to other nodes in the network. Each third party node processes each packet individually. In packet switching, the data that is encapsulated in the packet is evaluated and analyzed by the receiving node, so the data itself does not need to be completely reassembled and rebuilt by each node. Instead, packets are processed as needed. When data arrives at the destination node, it can be reassembled and delivered to the corresponding destination device. In this way, when the data is finally delivered to the destination node, only the original destination device can understand the received data. This approach ensures that data can be transmitted securely and efficiently.

In the transmitter, data arrives at the input lines in the form of an address sequence. In addition, Baran suggested in the original article that each transmitted packet should have a unique identifier to allow all intermediate nodes to access their corresponding sequence.
At the third party nodes, the address tag is examined, the message block is evaluated, and a routing decision is made. Then, the message block is moved to the output line to which it is directed.
When the message block reaches the destination node, it is stored and transferred to the output line connected to the appropriate output line. The time it takes for the data to be forwarded in this way may vary.

The port is capable of handling cruise liners of up to 97m draft. A security check is operated at the wharf as a mandatory Australian Government Requirement for all persons disembarking and visitors to the area. Some ferries to Southport leave from here.
The New Farm Wharf transport hub is the most northerly of a series of railway terminals located along the Brisbane River waterfront, the others being west of New Farm at The Gabba, Woolloongabba, Kangaroo Point and Windsor. Here the rail terminus used to be in the form of an R4 metro platform alongside which the 1911 terminus of the Brisbane City railway line reached the wharf. In 1960 a R4 combined passenger/loading tram was put on this terminus. The tram loading service ceased in 1969.
In 1975 the terminus rail station closed and was replaced with a new R2 bus loading station and car parking area. The car park is split with one bay reserved for each R1 southbound and R2 northbound service loading. The bus loading R2 station was newly built beside the earlier turnpike R2 bus stand. For example, suppose we wish to determine whether two graphs Gand H have the same colored vertices. (This is a common situation because there is an obvious polynomial-time reduction from the colored graph isomorphism problem to the ordinary graph isomorphism problem.) The corresponding AM proof system goes as follows: If Gand H are in fact isomorphic, our oracle coin-flipper outputs coins C and our prover responds by providing a witness W that defines the bijection between G and H. The verifier first flips his coins C and receives the color of each vertex in G. Then the verifier asks the prover if the corresponding vertex in H has the same color. If the colors match, he accepts the response of the prover. Otherwise, he rejects the response of the prover.

Gloucester is a cathedral city and district of Gloucestershire, in the West of England. Gloucester occupies most of the eastern two-thirds of the River Severn valley. It has long been associated with the River Severn, as it is the deepest tidal riverport in Europe. It is considered the third-oldest city in England after London and York, and has a population of around 140,000. The city of Gloucester is surrounded by Gloucestershire, which is part of South West England, and is the seat of the Gloucester Diocese. The city and its surrounding area is also sometimes referred to as the "Forest of Gloucester", for the wooded undulations of the Cotswolds that surround it. 

Gloucester was founded as a Roman city, Colonia Glevensis, in the 1st century AD, and flourished in the Middle Ages. It has a legacy of stone buildings, and is dominated by its large cathedral and the Gothic ruins of Gloucester Castle. The city's historic Old Town was one of the best preserved in England and was a contributing factor to Gloucester's designation as one of England's first designated Heritage Cities. From the latter 19th century to early 21st century Gloucester had a relatively successful economy based on the development of ship building and the manufacturing of other forms of machinery. However, like most of the UK, Gloucester's economy is now concentrated on the service sector and public sector, both nationally and locally. These services are especially well represented in the large retail environment of the city and in the education sector, housing the University of Gloucestershire.

The historian Stefan WinVecte has argued for a three-region division of medieval Gloucestershire (subdividing the later Gloucestershire into Severn, Wye and Avonshire), which left significant potential for shifts in power on the margins of the district. The most telling demarcation ran between Gloucester and the Vale of Gloucester, along the ridge of hills separating the two areas. It was a marginal area through which power shifted; the River Severn was one of the three major trade routes in the country, and along with the Wye and the Avon formed a major nexus in the landscape. Other considerations of the valley are that it was oriented directly towards the city, and had potential to be defended by virtue of its abysmal topography. It is important to note, however, that the waterways only represented a small part of the city's trade and that the city is situated perfectly for trade throughout southern England.

Blockchain technology is revolutionizing the healthcare industry by enabling secure and transparent management of patient data, which was previously managed through centralized systems prone to data breaches and privacy concerns. Here’s a detailed look at how blockchain technology addresses these issues and enhances patient data management:

### Enhanced Security and Privacy

1. **Decentralization**: Unlike traditional databases, which are often centralized, blockchain stores data across a distributed network. This means that no single entity has control over the entire database, making it much more difficult for hackers to compromise the system. The use of cryptographic algorithms ensures that data is tamper-proof.

2. **Immutable Records**: Once data is recorded on the blockchain, it cannot be altered or deleted without the consensus of the network. This immutability is a critical aspect of security, ensuring that medical records remain unchanged and reliable.

3. **Patient Control**: Blockchain allows patients to have more control over their personal health data. Patients can grant access to their data only when necessary and can revoke access if they wish. This level of control significantly enhances privacy.

### Transparent Data Sharing

1. **Interoperability**: Blockchain enables seamless data sharing among healthcare providers, researchers, and patients. By using a common platform, it becomes easier for different healthcare institutions to access and share patient data securely, improving the coordination of care.

2. **Consensus Mechanisms**: The consensus algorithms used in blockchain ensure that all parties agree on the accuracy of the data. This transparency is crucial for clinical research, as it guarantees that the data used for analysis is valid and trustworthy.

3. **Auditability**: All transactions and changes to patient data are recorded on the blockchain, providing an audit trail. This feature ensures accountability and makes it easier to trace the origin and modification history of data, which is invaluable for legal and compliance purposes.

### Improved Data Integrity

1. **Verification**: The use of cryptographic hashes in blockchain ensures that data is verified and authenticated. This process ensures that the data being shared is genuine and has not been tampered with.

2. **Redundancy**: Since data is stored across multiple nodes in the network, it reduces the risk of data loss due to hardware failures or other single points of failure.

### Applications in Healthcare

1. **Electronic Health Records (EHRs)**: Blockchain can provide a secure platform for managing EHRs, allowing patients to control access while ensuring that healthcare providers can access the data when needed.

2. **Clinical Trials**: By using blockchain, clinical trial data can be securely shared and tracked, reducing the risk of data manipulation and ensuring that the results are accurate and reliable.

3. **Supply Chain Management**: Blockchain can be used to track medications and medical devices from manufacturing to distribution, ensuring that patients receive genuine and safe treatments.

In conclusion, the use of blockchain technology in healthcare significantly enhances the security, transparency, and integrity of patient data. By decentralizing data storage and ensuring immutability, blockchain addresses the privacy concerns associated with centralized systems. Furthermore, its interoperability and auditability features make it an ideal solution for managing patient data securely and efficiently.

The clinical pharmacist collaborates with the primary care provider to ensure patient safety, optimize drug therapy, increase patient adherence to prescribed medications, and increase overall patient safety. In addition, the pharmacist must be well versed in pharmaceutical chemistry to create the proper medications needed for patients when available medications are lacking or must be modified due to intolerance or interdose intervals. In addition, the clinical pharmacist is trained to perform these duties in multiple settings, including hospitals, long-term care facilities, ambulatory care centers, skilled nursing centers, home health organizations, and universities.
Job Requirements
Employers prefer to hire clinical pharmacists who have the following qualifications, which may include but are not limited to:
* Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD), which involves a minimum of four years of professional school following the completion of an undergraduate degree
* Some employers will require licensed and board-certified pharmacists with at least a bachelor's degree and five years of relevant experience
About the Work
Clinical pharmacists can provide direct patient care services in various settings and oversee other pharmacists and technicians in these settings. The clinical pharmacist conducts case studies, reviews patient charts and medication records, and provides consultations regarding drug interactions, compatibility issues, and contraindications. Clinical pharmacists work closely with patients to determine their medication needs. Clinical pharmacists also may provide other drug therapy services to the community or to groups of people in various settings. This work can also take place in a research environment, where pharmacists may develop, test, and evaluate new drugs.
Clinical pharmacists play a critical role in the healthcare industry as the population grows older and the cost of healthcare increases, the use of medications to treat various chronic diseases becomes a more common and preferred modality of care. In addition, a global interest in integrative medicine, where a pharmacist can use nature-derived substances (e.g., herbs and vitamins) to improve a patient's health, has contributed to the field's growth. Therefore, clinical pharmacists are in high demand in various settings and have the potential for excellent long-term job security.
Job Outlook
As a result of the growing aging population and increased use of medications for chronic conditions, the job outlook for clinical pharmacists is predicted to continue to grow. The mean wage for a clinical pharmacist in 2017 was $116,040 per year.
Job Responsibilities
Duties may include:
* Creating a comprehensive drug therapy plan for patients with complex drug therapy needs
* Developing and reviewing drug therapy plans
* Training healthcare professionals and students on drug therapy issues and matters
* Preparing patient-specific pharmaceutical knowledge resources
* Recommending evidence-based changes to various organizations' formularies and drug selection policies
* Making recommendations for medication compounding
* Educating and counseling patients on proper drug use
* Conducting pre- and post-discharge medication reviews
* Identifying and preventing drug-drug and drug-condition interactions
Job Characteristics
Clinical pharmacists must be licensed and meet all the following standards:
* Meet licensing requirements through passage of the North American Pharmacist Licensure Examination (NAPLEX) or Comprehensive Pharmacists Licensure Examination (CPLEX)
* Meet practical experience requirements
* Meet the character requirements specified by the board of pharmacy in their state of residency
Work Environment
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, clinical pharmacists practice in a variety of healthcare settings, including hospitals, long-term care facilities, ambulatory care centers, home health agencies, and universities.
In 2017, the largest employment was in ambulatory healthcare services, accounting for 57% of the total employment. The next largest was long-term care facilities (21%), followed by hospitals (19%) and retail pharmacies (3%).

\[ 100\% - 89.2\% = 10.8\% \]

Thus, the percentage of income held by the first 90% of earners is \(\boxed{10.8\%}\).

Pharmaceutical manufacturing
Manufacturing pharmaceutical products requires a broad range of techniques from unit operations and engineering in chemistry, chemical engineering, chemical technology, industrial chemistry, analytical chemistry, microbiology, and pharmacology. The manufacturing of pharmaceutical products is a multi-billion-dollar industry, accounting for jobs ranging from material science, engineering, manufacturing management, process engineering, control engineering, electrical engineering, and mechanics, among others.

The FDA requires manufacturers of any product claiming to be a drug (as defined by the FDCA) to obtain approval of each unique formulation prior to the drug going to market. Manufacturers can be the source of drugs in two ways: 1) the drugs are already being marketed in another country, or 2) the drugs have never been produced before, meaning that the manufacturer has no preexisting quality control and quality assurance (QA/QC) documentation for their products.

In the first case, the manufacturer submits an application that has already been approved by a foreign regulatory authority that follows guidelines similar to those of the FDA. The FDA typically checks for compliance with its cGMP and approval by a foreign authority in order for the application to be approved. This approval does not guarantee that the drug can be marketed, but only that the drug is safe for human consumption. If there are changes to a drug's structure, formulation, or method of manufacture, these changes must be supported by appropriate data similar to the information in the new drug application (NDA).

In the second case, manufacturers have to submit either a New Drug Application (NDA) or a Biologic License Application (BLA) as described above. The NDA must contain animal and clinical data for all relevant patient populations. An application is approved by the FDA through a combination of data from the sponsor and many government-inspected quality control and quality assurance data. Most drugs on the market today fall into this category.
