During a snowstorm, a helicopter carrying two NTSB (National Transportation Safety Board) members and Chris Wallace, host of "Fox News Sunday," crashed in rural central Pennsylvania, and all were killed. The helicopter had taken off from Capital Region International Airport in New York State at around 5:35 pm on its way to the scene of a accident on I-70 in Fulton County, in order to transport two crash investigators to the site for analysis. The crash occurred at 5:50 pm EST just two minutes after the aircraft left the airport, about 45 miles southwest of Harrisburg and 55 miles northwest of Scranton.
[Spencer Boudan/LNP]
In addition to Wallace, Jay DiAngelo and Todd Rafferty were killed in the crash. Rafferty and DiAngelo were passengers on the helicopter. The two investigators had spent the morning of the crash in Washington, D.C., participating in an industry safety meeting, according to an NTSB release. They were in Pennsylvania investigating a crash that occurred in November. Wallace had just finished hosting the final show of the day and was on his way back home, according to a statement from the station.
"All three were great friends, and I will miss them terribly," the statement read.
The cause of the helicopter's crash is under investigation. NTSB chairman Robert Sumwalt said Sunday evening that the NTSB has sent a team to the scene to investigate. Sumwalt told reporters that officials are still trying to determine the final weather conditions, which would be important to consider because it's possible the helicopter may have taken off even though visibility was below the minimum requirements. The helicopter "shouldn't have flown in those conditions," according to Sumwalt.
The craft had taken off from Buffalo, New York, and had flown in and out of Washington, D.C., and Philadelphia, according to a social media post by a local Pennsylvania news station. Its flight path took it over Gettysburg and into the foothills of the Poconos. The pilot had been based out of the Philadelphia area and had about 5,600 hours of flying experience, according to FAA records.
The helicopter wreckage came to rest near Wilbur Twp. on State Route 132. The wind on Sunday was gusting to 25 mph, according to wind readings taken at an airport near the site of the crash. Although the pilot likely would have known the visibility was below the minimum requirements, pilots can occasionally take off despite bad visibility, according to Richard Aboulafia, an aerospace analyst with Teal Group.
The United States has no industry standard governing how pilots should respond to bad weather, but it is an industry norm for pilots to make sure they have enough visibility to see the end of the runway as they take off, Aboulafia said. So it's possible the pilot did not stop the helicopter at Buffalo based on bad weather visibility and instead took off after getting adequate information about the weather in Pennsylvania.
The visibility and turbulence on Sunday were notably below normal. Thursday night saw visibility at the Harrisburg airport at 10 miles, which is just below the 12-mile visibility threshold. That weather persisted into Sunday.
While weather forecasters indicated it was 95 percent likely that there would be less than five miles of visibility Sunday night, it's possible that by the time the aircraft was taking off, the visibility fell below acceptable levels. The helicopter pilot will likely play a role in the investigation.
The helicopter took off from a new ramp that was recently completed at the Capital Region Airport, and which is owned by the Wilbur Township Chamber of Commerce. The length of the runway is 4,901 feet, according to aviation specialists. While the runway is not long enough for a commercial aircraft, it could handle a helicopter. Commercial aircraft have a much longer stopping distance than a helicopter, which means they need runways with greater distances. The ramp in Wilbur Township was new, and officials only purchased the air charter, which ran about $200,000, in November.
Pilot Craig Hamilton had recently graduated from helicopter pilot school in 2015. He just got his license in October 2016. He had 5,600 total hours, of which about 230 were in IFR conditions, when he last flew an aircraft, according to FAA records.
Reports also said the flight was carrying six people, which matches the number of people killed in the crash.

Pilots tend to be given less responsibility for navigating through turbulence because they are flying small aircraft, Aboulafia said.

In 1965, with the approval of the Florida State Legislature, the local government abolished its traditional city and county government, which had existed since the early years of the state. The city expanded its limits to 1,644,716 acres (665,464 ha) and renamed itself a "metropolitan municipality" ("non-statutory county"). That same year, voters approved placing up to three more home rule charters on the ballot during November 1968 elections. Voters authorized it to be voted on in their own separate election, leading to a city-only charter in 1969 (which was repealed in 1983 by the Florida Legislature in Jacksonville City Charter Repeal Act), a county-only charter in 1969, and a "combined municipal and county" charter to be voted on again. The 1969 "combined municipal and county" charter failed to pass.
For the next decade, negotiations between the County Commission, represented by its Chair, Randy French, and the City Commission were unsuccessful. Later that year, Jacksonville city and Duval County voters passed a referendum to establish a consolidated government, which required an overall majority of both counties to pass. ##### History
While recently annexed, parts of Sunnyside were once a large, rural farm owned by Charles Young. Many of the roads and highways in the area were established by his family. Early established roads include Kings Canyon Avenue, and Clovis Avenue, (originally nicknamed, "Clovisville Road"). It has since been named after nearby California's 31st governor, Earl Warren. Additional roads established by the Young family include, Empire Avenue, Griswold Avenue, and Mervyn Avenue, the latter of which connects Kings Canyon with the Mervyn Middle School.

Sunnyside received its name, in 1963, when the neighborhood was rebranded as Sunnyside-Highland, to prevent the city from annexing the remaining residential land for industrial use. Development in the neighborhood ceased, until a boost in industrialization in the 1980s brought mixed residential-industrial areas.

Later, after Proposition 227 passed in 1998, and the building of the Sunnyside Educational Development Corporation (SEDC), the housing market saw explosive growth, and nearly every lot in the neighborhood had a house built, though later 2000's recession brought the production down.
The area has been home to many ethnic residents, particularly Russian-Americans, and several cultural organizations, such as, the Fresno Russian-American Soccer Club. Following a 4-3 decision, the Supreme Court ruled the NCAA "crosses the line" in restricting schools from paying athletes. It said the restrictions are impermissible and are being used to allow an intermediary—like the NCAA—to increase its revenue. It also said that the NCAA can't stop schools from offering students things that states allow.
"For that reason," the justices wrote, "that revenue enhancement cannot be construed as education-related financial aid under the antitrust laws."
During oral argument on November 4, justices said they believed the NCAA "has no legal right to impose a rule that would otherwise be anticompetitive." Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said, "The idea that the NCAA takes in revenue in the billions and the student-athletes don't benefit monetarily from their generating that revenue is a poor enforcement of contracts."
"The NCAA denies student-athletes the right to use their market value to make a choice as to which college they would attend or to supplement any college funds their parents had for their education. That offends me, as an educator," Justice Brett Kavanaugh said during argument.
In a point of order, Justice Stephen Breyer challenged UCLA law professor Ernest Young's testimony that NCAA scholarship payments are educational funds rather than salaries: "Educational, he says, meaning scholarships. But, of course, like any scholarship, if you have a nonacademic education—that is, a sporting education—can't you use it to go somewhere else?"
The court's decision was in response to the NCAA, Pac-12 Conference, and Big Ten Conference's attempt to stop nearly 250 colleges and universities from giving current and recently graduated athletes as much as $5,600 a year in scholarships for "education-related costs" over the next four years. With California's new law in effect, the question has now shifted to the NCAA and which colleges and universities will sue to have the law rolled back.
Pac-12 spokesman Greg Carl said the conference would meet "in the coming days" to discuss how to move forward, calling the court's decision a "significant development." Big Ten spokesman Mike Wolohan said in an email, "As always, we plan to respect the rules of the [anti-trust] litigation."
"The courts have sided with this common-sense proposition and are allowing athletes to earn more for the time and effort they put in to help their schools succeed," said NCAA CEO Mark Emmert.
#### The Institution Needs to Change
The NCAA has to get the message, and it's not getting it, argues Kevin Fitzgerald, a former Notre Dame linebacker and 10-year NFL running back.
"Our system rewards the wrong behaviors," he writes for Yahoo Sports. "The biggest reward goes to colleges that eschew academics for success on the field. The super-competitive schools in the football-focused Big Ten and the Big 12 are at the top of the food chain. The concern of not having another [television] contract reigned supreme. They figured out the system—they hoard available coaches. They take early signing periods to exploit young talent, and they are able to do that because they have the power within the system. They don't make that power available to the next big thing, nor the next one after that.
"The C-USA, the Mountain West, the Sun Belt are at the bottom of the food chain, competing against what seems like the natural order of things—big money on the field paying athletes big time. This is unsustainable."
Big time college sports have become more than the game or the competition, it has become a giant business operated by the NCAA. An industry.
#### This is Big Business
"The recent court ruling will make the impact of the NCAA's business practices noticeable in the near future," writes Jeff Knox. "California gave athletes the ability to benefit from their NIL [name, image and likeness] rights while Florida gave athletes the ability to unionize while maintaining their amateur status. There were several college sports that saw money or total NIL rules put into place. Just think back to a few years ago where the NCAA wouldn't allow athletic department to pay players."
Knox points out "the NCAA could lose a huge chunk of its revenue, which has been largely coming from a piece of the action that college athletes could potentially earn on their own."
Even if the NCAA's protest falls on deaf ears, someone within the organization needs to realize that their policies need to be overhauled.
The thought that led to the change of colleges and universities giving players and scholarship athletes NIL opportunities may be to revamp its position on amateurism. In 2015, the NCAA changed its rules to ensure "college athletes cannot be paid for representing their school," with the restriction that athletes are not allowed to be paid.
"When the NCAA considered changes in 2014 to allow NIL, its rules committee recommended banning athletes from earning compensation based on NIL opportunities for financial gain."
The NCAA is slowly recognizing its mistakes and the fact it needs to change its policies in order to remain relevant. The growing amount of athletes receiving $5,600 scholarships could be a sign of that change.
#### Change Doesn't Change the Fact
Despite the new court decision, the evidence still proves the idea of the NCAA has been "tainted."
Dave Zirin points out, "As with most things, white supremacy remains the key driver of change in the world of college sports.
"The NCAA's primary constituency will be elite, predominantly white men's sports and the power structure that upholds the rule book of sport that is white."
Both the NFL and NBA have stopped themselves before they went too far. Now, a generation of amateur athletes will be better prepared to make a living on and off the field.
"It's clear to me the NCAA will never be a real school when it comes to the actual university experience," writes NFL running back Alex Smith. "Coaches and administrators will continue to exploit student athletes' intellect and physical abilities for their own benefit. All of us agree what's in the best interest of student athletes. But it is not the NCAA."
The NCAA should have known better. Most of these players have used the NCAA for their own benefit.
#### It's Where the Money Is
Money is involved in NCAA decision-making, and in the future, many speculate those looking to gain economic advantage from that involvement will get the upper hand. Is there a better example of this than the matter of former Notre Dame football coach Knute Rockne's "hail Mary pass" to Southern California's Zombie Stadium for a game in 1928?
"In every other playoff selection committee, members are paid in one way or another. A government official is often involved, and there is always money exchanging hands," writes Kevin Krugman in the Boston College sports blog Fighting the Light. "However, in the NCAA, the decision-makers are unpaid, which places them at a huge disadvantage."
The National Association of Basketball Coaches paid for tickets to all of the games it recommended for inclusion in the tournament. To protect itself, it used Delaware Inland Bypass, a nonprofit operating under federal law, and says it provided minimal services.
"Still, the NCAA said it did not pay for the tickets and that if it was shown that they did, there would be consequences."
Krugman continues, "There is no question that tickets are the wild card in the tournament selection process. They can be used as a tool for commissioners to gain favor with the membership of the men's basketball committee."
Prior to 1999, the tournament was reserved for the 32 winning teams in the AP Poll. The conference tournaments were looking to add teams as a boost for television contracts.
Since the NCAA runs these tournaments, it provided the opportunity and the venues. But, it is something where the board "wants to put the tools in the hands of the coaches and the school to pick themselves into the tournament," says former NCAA commissioner Jim Breyer.
"I just think the selection process needs to be very transparent, with clear expectations and very clear guidance," says Breyer. "We really made mistakes early in the process and a lot of transparency was asked for."
If this was being done outside of the NCAA, it would be illegal to bribe a sports tournament selection committee with high-priced tickets. All sports, specifically, NCAA basketball, are looking to gain more profit, including the most profitable conference—the ACC.
"Overall, the ACC reported $74.3 million in revenue during the 2018 season, 16 percent more than in 2017. Basketball was the top revenue generator, logging $26.2 million—29 percent more than in 2017, according to NCAA documents provided to The Associated Press."
What was the source of all this money, and to what was it donated? With all of the salaries paid to the coaching staffs and the administration staff, how could it not be to the individual conference?
#### After the NCAA rained on this parade
When these financial decisions are in the hands of individuals with sports experience, the athletes will become more valuable over time. The NCAA's purpose was to "protect" these athletes, but it looks more like an attempt to bury them.
Brandon Crouch, an actor that plays football at Cal State Fullerton, wrote to the New York Times about his experience with the NCAA: 
"I spent eight years of my life playing for scholarships that I couldn't earn or keep. As a result, I went into a financially worse position. Yet, I stayed at the table and was more prepared in my life than I would have been without the NCAA."
Follow any sports conference to understand that in the fall and spring, those 12 months of the year all revolve around football or basketball; rest is taken in the summer. The NCAA allows for other educational things, but the priority is the games. I'm not exaggerating.
The best possible way to do this would be to put the real learning opportunities in the hands of professors from that department,

The section of Huntington Boulevard between First Street on the west to Cedar Avenue on the east is the home to many large, stately homes. The tract's boundaries were Balch Avenue on the south, Cedar Avenue on the east, the rear property line of Platt Avenue (east of Sixth Street) and Platt Avenue (west of Sixth Street) on the north, and First Street on the west. At the time of its admission to the City, the Alta Vista Tract was uninhabited but landscaped, although the trees had to be watered by tank wagon. In 1914 developers Billings & Meyering acquired the tract, completed street development, provided the last of the necessary municipal improvements including water service, and began marketing the property with fervor. A mere half decade later the tract had 267 homes. This rapid development was no doubt hastened by the Fresno Traction Company right-of-way along Huntington Boulevard, which provided streetcar connections between downtown and the County Hospital.

# Bash Shell Script Task

## Task 1: Bash Shell Script for Hashmap

### Objective:
Write a Bash shell script to simulate a hashmap with basic operations: insertion, deletion, retrieval, and checking if an item exists.

### Requirements:
1. The script should accept input in the format "command key value" or "command key".
2. `command` can be `insert`, `delete`, `search`, or `check`.
3. If `value` is not provided with `insert`, the script should default to using the `key` as the value.
4. The script should store key-value pairs in an associative array.
5. It should provide feedback (success or failure) for each operation.
6. Ensure proper handling of invalid commands.

### Example usage:
```bash
./map.sh insert 1 2
./map.sh insert 3
./map.sh search 1
./map.sh search 3
./map.sh delete 1
./map.sh check 3
```

### Sample Output:
```
Inserted key: 1 with value: 2
Inserted key: 3 with value: 3
Found key: 1 with value: 2
Found key: 3 with value: 3
Deleted key: 1
Found key: 3 with value: 3
```

### Implementation:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

declare -A map

while true; do
    read -p "Enter command, key, and value (or just 'key' for check): " command key value
    case "$command" in
        insert)
            if [ -z "$value" ]; then
                value=$key
            fi
            map["$key"]="$value"
            echo "Inserted key: $key with value: $value"
            ;;
        delete)
            if [[ -n ${map["$key"]} ]]; then
                unset map["$key"]
                echo "Deleted key: $key"
            else
                echo "Key $key does not exist."
            fi
            ;;
        search)
            if [[ -n ${map["$key"]} ]]; then
                echo "Found key: $key with value: ${map["$key"]}"
            else
                echo "Key $key does not exist."
            fi
            ;;
        check)
            if [[ -n ${map["$key"]} ]]; then
                echo "Key $key exists."
            else
                echo "Key $key does not exist."
            fi
            ;;
        *)
            echo "Invalid command. Please use insert, delete, search, or check."
            ;;
    esac
done
```

For example, if a wire is being moved downward through a magnetic field, the induced voltage will be in the same direction as the wire, flowing from the bottom of the wire to the top.

The climate of the Tibet Autonomous Region, located in western China, is on average the coldest of any region within China, with very little annual rainfall. Tibetan climate is characterised by wide diurnal temperature variation during most of the year. Winters are extremely cold with temperatures in Lhasa typically below 0 °C (32 °F) and the nights often below −10 °C (14 °F). Temperatures are somewhat warmer at lower altitudes but the temperature declines faster with altitude in Tibet than most mountainous areas. Lhasa typically sees only about 125 warm days (days above 20 °C or 68 °F) a year, one of the few locales in the world with less than 100 warm days (despite its low latitude near the Himalayan foothills). Annual precipitation in Lhasa averages about 460 mm (18 in) and is very variable, since precipitation is very uncertain and sporadic in much of Tibet. Most of the precipitation is rainfall during the summer months, but amounts are very small (typically less than 100 mm or 4 in). Snowfall is sporadic but occasionally heavy. Summers, except at high elevations, are cool to warm, averaging only about 10–22 °C (50–72 °F), and are extremely wet, with average humidity above 80%. At high elevations, during the warm season, temperatures commonly drop below freezing at night, and snow can fall even in July. Lhasa records an average of 106 nights a year with temperatures below freezing.

The ordinary legislative procedure
The ordinary legislative procedure was created by the Single European Act. It provides for the Commission to make a proposal, which the Council then adopts by qualified majority voting. If the Council does not adopt the proposal by the time agreed, the Commission may make a second proposal, which the Council has to adopt by the end of the time agreed by qualified majority voting. If the Council has refused to adopt a Commission proposal by qualified majority voting, the Parliament can adopt a legislative resolution that the Commission shall adopt, if the resolution is voted for by an absolute majority of the members of Parliament. The qualified majority in the Council must then adopt a decision that accepts the legislative resolution of the Parliament.
The budgetary procedure
Budgets and other community financial measures are adopted under the budgetary procedure. It requires an agreement between the Parliament and the Council and requires the Commission's consent. The process starts with a Commission proposal. The Council must vote by unanimity by 14 November or otherwise by the Budgetary Control Committee of the Parliament by 31 December. Parliament must vote by a two-thirds majority of those members present. If the budget is not adopted by the deadline, the most recent adopted budget is extended. If the extended budget is not adopted, the previous year's budget is extended for a period of one year.
The new financial perspective
The new financial perspective for the period 2007–2013 will shift the focus to the intake of money to the community, including from non-EU countries, instead of expenditure. This will be due to the external impact and quality of the EU's policies. This will mean a much bigger trade, industrial, market and economic policy within the EU, with many new countries joining the union. The focus will move from merely tax and equal economic rules, to market liberalisation. Equality in social, health and environmental conditions will grow. European policies will not just be about goods: services, funds and people. This is all to be decided and agreed by the European Council. In addition, the relative powers of the national governments and parliaments will be decided and agreed by the European Council, a process known as subsidiarity. This will, in effect, bring about the social and economic transition of the 21st-century EU economy.

# Using the [Docker Multi-Stage Build](https://docs.docker.com/develop/develop-images/multistage-build/) feature with TypeScript and Electron. 

This guide demonstrates how to build an Electron application using multi-stage builds in Docker. The electron-react-boilerplate tutorial app will be used as a reference.

- `FROM node:10.11 AS builder`
- `WORKDIR /usr/src/app`
- `COPY package*.json .`
- `RUN npm install`
- `COPY . .`
- `RUN npm run build-electron-main && npm run build-electron-render`
- `FROM node:10.11`
- `COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/build /usr/src/app/build`
- `COPY . /usr/src/app`
- `WORKDIR /usr/src/app`
- `EXPOSE 8443`
- `CMD [ "npm", "run", "start-electron" ]`

How do these two features work together to build the application, and how does the final image differ from a standard single-stage build?

The Docker multi-stage build feature allows for a more streamlined and efficient build process by using multiple images and stages to create the final image. This guide demonstrates how to use multi-stage builds with TypeScript and Electron to build an Electron application.

The first stage, named "builder", starts with the `node:10.11` base image, copies the `package*.json` files into the `/usr/src/app` directory, installs the dependencies using `npm install`, and then copies the rest of the application files into the same directory. This stage builds the application using the `build-electron-main` and `build-electron-render` commands.

The second stage starts with the `node:10.11` base image and copies the compiled Electron application from the first stage into the `/usr/src/app/build` directory. It then copies the rest of the application files from the first stage into the same directory. Finally, it sets the working directory to `/usr/src/app`, exposes port `8443`, and specifies the command to run the Electron application using the `start-electron` script.

By using multi-stage builds, the final image is smaller and more optimized than a standard single-stage build because it only includes the necessary files and dependencies. In this case, the final image will only contain the compiled Electron application and the Node.js runtime. Additionally, it ensures that the production build is used in the final image, rather than the development build, by building the application in a separate stage. This results in a smaller and faster image that can be easily deployed and run.

Why are alpha and beta created? Why are stocks considered risky? An individual can invest in say company A, but they may also invest in company B.
The problem with investing in both company A and B, is that if one of them performs bad (i.e. due to a bad decision made by the manager) the other one is likely to do so as well. So in this way portfolio diversification helps. Now if a given portfolio diversification cannot mitigate the risk, which is often the case, what exactly are alpha and beta for? Are they an investment opportunity, i.e. if you knew the level of an asset's alpha or beta you could at least somewhat judge its future performances?

Background
Financial risk means that outcome variables (i.e. returns) have uncertainty. This uncertainty can be due to market events and firm-specific events (see e.g. Scott, J.E. (1983). « Quantification and the measurement of risk ». Accounting, Organizations and Society, 8(4): 299-306). The former are asset-specific but they may affect many firms. An example might be a large technological breakthrough that changes industry structure. The latter are firm-specific (see e.g. Meyer, R.K., Myers, S.C. and Zingales, L. (2000). « MIR: Measurement, Incentives and Research ». Journal of Finance, 55(4): 1467-1520). These risk factors arise because of idiosyncratic events and problems or because of mismanagement. 
What is Risk?
Usually, risk is estimated by calculating standard deviation which is measured as the square root of the variance of returns (Econometric Theory, George B. Maudlin, 2007, page 15). This is called historical risk and is a backward looking measure. However, risk is a forward looking measure, i.e. measures are based on forecasts. These measures of risk are called market risk measures and are calculated as a function of the covariance or correlation between each stocks’ return and the market return. This amount of risk is often called Beta (β). It describes the level of systematic or market risk that is inherent in a security. If the correlation of stock and market return is zero it implies that the stock movement is independent from the market returns, i.e. its risk will not change with market movements. Any kind of risk that cannot be attributed to a specific or common factor is called idiosyncratic risk.
Assessing Risk
There are many measures available to assess risk. Standard deviation is not used very often nowadays because it fails to differentiate between periods of positive and negative returns. In the case of an investor investing in multiple assets (i.e. multiple securities) instead of in a single asset it might reduce or eliminate risk through diversification. The firm specific risk can be reduced or eliminated with this portfolio diversification. Moreover, it has also been shown that even the exposure to systematic risk can be minimized through diversification. On this point of firm specific risk, a good way to think about risk in the first place is knowing how risky is your investment (i.e. returns). Risk is how you’re going to finance your returns. Olympics

The activities at the sports centre in the Battersea Powerhouse will also be extended and confirmed as there will be new space for classes such as Zumba and Yoga.

The development of the Attenborough Arts Centre and the former Arcola Theatre in Southwark will both also move forward.

Another major feature of the complexity of construction is the large number of parties involved in the project. Most construction projects involve at least one owner (such as an individual or a corporation), a general contractor, construction company or construction manager, and dozens of subcontractors for different elements of the construction. Those entities sometimes find it possible to bring outside counsel, but mostly those individuals involved in the project work with a project manager or construction lawyer on contract drafting, review and negotiation. Issues related to issues of right of entry, compliance, and insurance issues frequently arise, and contractors and project owners must develop a working relationship from the outset in order to avoid significant issues later.
There is also, in the United States, a culture that is very successful when it comes to negotiating construction contracts. The American culture of the West does not encourage the back and forth nature of contract negotiations with a small number of parties, but rather, the American contractor’s approach to contract negotiations is designed to provide maximum flexibility while avoiding risky agreements with subcontractors and suppliers. This culture does not mean that there are not a number of practices in place that are less than transparent. For example, some construction companies will charge subcontractors their own percentage on the value of the subcontractor’s work. A company must be careful in its negotiation practices, as those individuals engaged in the contracting process may not wish to follow the contractual provisions. Further, subcontractors are often only notified after the work has been completed, and this may not reflect the terms of the contract itself.
A case law
There are a number of cases dealing with the design of a construction contract. In the United States, parties must adopt a standard industry form agreement, the standard form of which is determined by local law. There is a common theme in a number of different standard industry forms of agreement, which is that some parties are generally treated favorably, with some being granted an advantage in some instances over others. These standards are not exhaustive, and there are a number of other provisions which are not covered by the standard form of contract. However, there are a number of important provisions which may not necessarily be covered by the standard form, which may be covered by a narrower standard. In the United States, the standard form of construction contract is generally more structured and well thought out than a standard form of construction contract is in most other countries, and as a result, the standard form of construction contract is not generally adopted by industry-wide firms.

Many subcontractors are engaged through a large number of employees. Employees are hired by general contractors, construction companies, construction managers and subcontractors, and typically work for one employer. In this situation, contracting parties will generally be named in the employer’s contract, and the contracting parties will have no independent authority to sign agreements with the subcontractors.

In such a case, the contracting parties may be named in the contract, and the contracting parties may have the right to assign the contract to the subcontractor, thereby avoiding the risk of further litigation.

Document: Laser interstitial thermal therapy
Laser interstitial thermal therapy, often called LITT, is a minimally invasive procedure for treating intracranial pathology. Under either local or general anesthesia, the surgeon inserts a laser probe into the target lesion or lesion bed (if the lesion has been removed) and delivers a pulse of laser energy to ablate the affected brain tissue (i.e. tumor or epileptogenic zone). LITT is currently available at a limited number of specialized centers globally. It is performed by interventional neuroradiologists, neurosurgeons, and neuro-sterotacticians.
The most recent literature has reported nearly 100% one-year survival in treated patients with limited surgical risks with various variants of ablation devices being utilized. NCCN guidelines consider LITT to be an option for the treatment of recurrent gliomas in cases where reoperation is considered a futile treatment.
Oncologic safety has been reported to be optimal, with less than 0.1% of patients experiencing an extratumoral or functional injury.
LITT at present is a technique considered for gliomas (and neuro-oncology lesions) and interstitial inflammation when the following circumstances are met:
Patient is not a candidate for traditional open surgery (e.g., patient has recurrent gliomas after multiple surgeries, has unmanageable risks, or has multiple comorbidities that preclude open brain surgery)
Patient has tumor in a sub-lobar part of the brain in which surgical resection would be on the edge of the surgery's margin or the surgeon would be unable to leave a sub-millimetric margin.
Patient has tumor(s) close to eloquent structures, if the risk of neurological disability from surgery is considerable.

Oxygen can be stored in three forms, as a liquified gas using vacuum-insulated tanks, as anhydrous (water-free) liquid in cryogenic tanks using a multilayer vacuum insulation system, or as a solid compacted using carbon molecular sieves, and stored in vacuum insulated tanks.[citation needed] The most common method is to use a cryogenic vacuum insulated tank storing it as a liquid.[citation needed]
The minimum liquid boiling temperature of oxygen under one atmosphere of pressure is −182.98 °C (90.18 K or −297.36 °F).
In industry, most liquid oxygen is produced with the use of cryogenic air separation plants, although in small quantities it can be produced by electrolysis of water.
Oxygen was discovered on 18th May 1774 by French chemist, Joseph Priestley in Wiltshire. Priestley is the very first person credited with discovering oxygen, however there is a debate in the scientific world as to whether the German-Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele or the British Scientist Joseph Priestley should be given the actual credit for the discovery.
The dispute has been discussed since Priestley is known to have written to Scheele to tell him the results of his experiments. In Priestley's 1775 book, titled "Observations on different kinds of Air," he details an experiment which describes a process very similar to how oxygen was discovered a few years before it was published. 
Due to the description of this book and the letter that was sent to Scheele, Priestley is credited with the discovery of oxygen.
During the next two years, he investigates and further details the properties of oxygen. His research focuses primarily on the chemical properties of the colorless and odorless gas, identifying that it supports life and that plants and animals produce it during the photosynthesis process.
Upon publishing his findings, Priestley's discoveries gain some popularity; however, he becomes the subject of ridicule due to his denomination as a Methodist. His work and life are even linked to William Blake and his famous poem "The Tyger." These discussions, debates and rejections continue for many years after his publication of "Observations on different kinds of Air".
The ultimate result is that Priestley is credited with discovering oxygen but his acceptance is hindered by many questioning who should receive credit for discovering oxygen.

He discovered that the purified gas he obtained facilitated respiration and combustion better than regular air. This new gas, which he coined "dephlogisticated air," would later be recognized as oxygen.

Producing oxygen on a large scale often involves the use of air separation plants, specifically large and complex equipment designed to extract oxygen from the air we breathe. These plants operate through processes such as pressure swing adsorption (PSA), membrane separation, and distillation techniques. Each method leverages differences in the physical properties of gases to effectively separate oxygen from the rest of the air components.

These plants are vital in ensuring a continuous supply of oxygen in industries ranging from steel production to pharmaceuticals. The efficiency of these facilities is paramount, given the sheer demand for oxygen in many industrial applications. Moreover, these plants help maintain the quality of oxygen by removing impurities like argon and nitrogen, thus providing a cleaner and more pure form of the gas.

In the context of oxygen storage, cylinders play a crucial role. These are typically pressure vessels designed to safely contain oxygen in a gaseous state under high pressure. Oxygen cylinders are indispensable in medical settings, where they provide supplemental oxygen to patients, aiding in respiration and supporting life in critical conditions.

Cylinders are also used extensively in industrial applications, such as welding and cutting processes, where a high flow rate of oxygen is required for efficient material processing. In these contexts, the design and safety features of oxygen cylinders ensure that they remain secure and reliable, contributing significantly to operational efficiency.

The history of oxygen's discovery and its subsequent industrial applications exemplifies a fascinating interaction between scientific discovery, technological innovation, and practical utility. For a welcome lunch, Zelda and her siblings pick up a 15 piece pizza, a 12 piece pizza and a 6-piece pizza. How many people can have one piece of pizza?

For a family reunion, Samantha decides to make a 36 piece pizza, a 12 piece pizza, and 26 individually made pizzas. How many people can have one slice of pizza in total?

To determine how many people can have one piece of pizza, we need to find the total number of pizza pieces and then add them together. Let's calculate step by step.

**For Zelda and her siblings:**
1. The 15 piece pizza has 15 pieces.
2. The 12 piece pizza has 12 pieces.
3. The 6 piece pizza has 6 pieces.

Adding these pieces together:
\[ 15 + 12 + 6 = 33 \]

So, Zelda and her siblings can have one piece of pizza for \(\boxed{33}\) people.

**For Samantha's family reunion:**
1. The 36 piece pizza has 36 pieces.
2. The 12 piece pizza has 12 pieces.
3. The 26 individually made pizzas each have 1 piece, so \(26 \times 1 = 26\) pieces.

Adding these pieces together:
\[ 36 + 12 + 26 = 74 \]

So, Samantha can serve one piece of pizza for \(\boxed{74}\) people.

The function should return a tuple containing the indices of these critical points in the input list.

### Example
```
>>> identify_critical_points([[2, 3], [0, 0], [4, 0], [-1, -1]])
(1, 0)
```

### Note
In the example, the point with the minimum x-coordinate is [0, 0] and the point with the minimum y-coordinate is [-1, -1]. Hence, the function returns (1, 0).

### Constraints
* 1 <= points <= 1000
* -10^9 <= points[i][j] <= 10^9
* All x and y coordinates are unique.

from typing import List, Tuple

def identify_critical_points(points: List[List[float]]) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """
    Identifies the critical points on a smooth manifold in a 2D space given a list of points.
    These critical points are the absolute minimum and maximum coordinates in terms of x and y values from the list of points.
    The function returns a tuple containing the indices of these critical points in the input list.
    """
    min_index = max_index = 0
    for i in range(1, len(points)):
        if points[i][0] < points[min_index][0] or points[i][1] < points[min_index][1]:
            min_index = i
        if points[i][0] > points[max_index][0] or points[i][1] > points[max_index][1]:
            max_index = i
    return min_index, max_index

    print("All tests passed!")

check_function()

Saturn V (also known as Saturn V or SA-500C) was an American heavy-lift launch vehicle designed to send astronauts to the Moon in Project Apollo. It carried the Apollo command and service module complex to Low Earth orbit (LEO) and then the Apollo Command Module to the Moon, where an Apollo Lunar Module would be docked and land on the Moon. The Saturn V also carried several American satellites into geostationary orbit, including the Skylab space station and several others for NASA and the US Department of Defense (DoD). It was assembled on the Mobile Launch Complex in Florida and fired from the Kennedy Space Center.

The vehicle was composed of three main stages and a towering launch tower. The tower carried the spacecraft into LEO, where a second launch to the Moon occurred, usually on a smaller (two or three engines) stage and its own spacecraft: a Lunar Module (LM) and a Lunar Module Adapter (LMA). The LM would be the only stage to reach the lunar surface, after which it would be used to ascend and dock with the Command Module (CM) in lunar orbit. For the Apollo 11 and Apollo 17 missions, it was also used for the Apollo Ascent Propulsion Stage (APS), which fired in LEO before sending the command module on its way to the Moon. Each Apollo AS stage that fired had 1,300,000 kilograms (2,900,000 lb) of propellant to use to make a precision burn into the Earth-Moon transfer orbit (EATO), but it weighed only about 50,000 kilograms (110,000 lb) at take-off from the Moon's surface.

The vehicle consisted of three large stages (designated S-IC, S-II, and S-IVB) and four auxiliary Solid Rocket Boosters (SRBs). The five stages had five engines each, yielding a total of 13 engines. The number of engines in each stage is a product of a von Braun, Callahan and Meyer design philosophy which called for many small simple engines rather than a few complex ones, resulting in a design more likely to succeed and requiring more engine knowledge on the part of the designer.

The first stage, S-IC, was fully powered with RP-1/Aerozine 50 (hypergolic) engine

The second stage, S-II, was powered by five engines fueled by liquid hydrogen and LOX, the same as the S-IC, but without the Aerozine 50.

The third stage, S-IVB, was also powered by five engines fueled by liquid hydrogen and LOX. Four of the engines were used to power the spacecraft in lunar orbit, but the fifth engine was later used in the Apollo 11 and Apollo 17 missions to power the spacecraft in its orbit around the Moon. The main engine was later used for further burns, especially in the early stages of space travel.

The four SRBs, also known as auxiliary engines or staged rocket boosters (SRBs) were separately controlled and operated by the main vehicle control. They were designed to burn for 140 seconds, but the maximum time for fuel burnout was 120 seconds. The first stage is the most powerful of all the stages, with over 5 million pound-force (22.33 tonnes) of thrust.

import re

def extract_text_from_latex(latex_code):
    pattern = r'\\begin\{document\}(.+?)\\end\{document\}'
    match = re.search(pattern, latex_code, re.DOTALL)
    if match:
        text = match.group(1)
        text = re.sub(r'\\[a-z]+', '', text)  # Remove LaTeX commands
        return text.strip()  # Remove leading/trailing whitespace
    else:
        return None

# Example usage
latex_input = r"""
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
Lorem Ipsum is simply dummy text of the printing and typesetting industry. Lorem Ipsum has been the industry's standard dummy text ever since the 1500s, when an unknown printer took a galley of type and scrambled it to make a type specimen book. It has survived not only five centuries, but also the leap into electronic typesetting, remaining essentially unchanged. It was popularised in the 1960s with the release of Letraset sheets containing Lorem Ipsum passages, and more recently with desktop publishing software like Aldus PageMaker including versions of Lorem Ipsum.
\end{document}
"""

plain_text_output = extract_text_from_latex(latex_input)
print(plain_text_output)
```

### Discussion of "Computational complexity theory" in relation to "polynomial time algorithm"
In computational complexity theory, a key concern is the efficiency of algorithms. The time taken by an algorithm to solve a problem often depends on the size of the input, denoted as n. One critical aspect is whether the time complexity of the algorithm can be described by a polynomial function of n. An algorithm whose time complexity is a polynomial in n is known as a polynomial time algorithm. This concept is central to determining whether a problem is efficiently solvable by a computer. Problems that can be solved by a polynomial time algorithm are considered tractable or feasible to compute within a reasonable amount of time as the input grows.

### Discussion of "Computational complexity theory" in relation to "Cobham's thesis"
Cobham's thesis, proposed by the British computer scientist Michael O. Rabin, offers a formal definition of what it means for a problem to be computationally feasible. According to this thesis, a problem is considered feasible to compute if and only if it can be solved in polynomial time. The idea behind Cobham's thesis is that any practical computation can be carried out within a polynomial time constraint. This perspective is fundamental to the area of computational complexity theory because it distinguishes between problems that can be feasibly solved and those that are not, based on the growth rate of the time required as the input size increases.

### Discussion of Interaction between "polynomial time algorithm" and "Cobham's thesis" in context of "Computational complexity theory"
The relationship between "polynomial time algorithm" and "Cobham's thesis" is inherently intertwined within the framework of "computational complexity theory". Cobham's thesis establishes the theoretical foundation for the classification of computational problems based on their time complexity. Specifically, it states that problems that can be solved using a polynomial time algorithm are the ones that are practically solvable. This direct link between the concept of a polynomial time algorithm and Cobham's thesis is crucial for understanding the classification of problems into complexity classes such as P (polynomial time), NP (nondeterministic polynomial time), and others. This interaction is central to the study of computational complexity as it provides a clear, mathematically precise boundary for what is considered to be computationally feasible and infeasible. 

Through this analysis, we see that "polynomial time algorithm" and "Cobham's thesis" serve as pillars in defining the boundaries of efficiency and feasibility in computation, which are fundamental considerations in "computational complexity theory". The interplay between these concepts helps guide the design and analysis of algorithms, enabling researchers and practitioners to make informed decisions about which problems can be practically solved and which ones cannot.

Newton's Third Law: Practical Applications and Discussion
The understanding of Newton's Third Law has led to numerous practical applications, including the development of rockets, propellers, and satellites. The law highlights the reciprocal nature of forces between objects, which is a fundamental principle in mechanics. A practical example of this law in action is the propulsion of a rocket. This interaction is perfectly described by Newton's Third Law. In essence, the rocket exerts a force on the exhaust gases (action), and in turn, the exhaust gases exert an equal and opposite force on the rocket (reaction). This unequal distribution of mass and momentum provides the necessary propulsion for the rocket to overcome Earth's gravity and achieve orbit.

A new study finds that eating blueberries slows memory loss in older adults.
To date, most research on the health benefits of blueberries has focused on how the fruit affects heart health, not the brain. This new report is among the first to zero in on the direct benefits for cognitive function.
“We have shown that just a single serving of blueberries, once a week, can slow cognitive decline in adults as they age,” Maria Villareal, one of the study’s authors and an assistant professor at Pennington Biomedical Research Center at Louisiana State University, said in a statement.
“It’s about 1 cup of blueberries a week. The results support adding blueberries to your diet if you want to boost your cognitive health,” she added.
For the study, researchers looked at about 40 participants (average age of 71) who were overweight and at risk for type 2 diabetes. All showed signs of mild cognitive impairment or memory loss, but none were diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. The researchers randomly assigned the participants to drink a daily smoothie with or without a serving of blueberries every week for 12 weeks.
Villareal and her team found that the blueberry-smoothie group performed better on a visual memory test than the group that didn’t have the fruit. The blueberry group also had a higher activity in a specific area of the brain related to visual memory.
The researchers believe that these results show that blueberries are “effective in lowering blood levels of pro-inflammatory biomarkers,” Villareal said. Increased inflammation has been linked to memory problems.
Interestingly, the study participants didn’t know which smoothie they got.
“Many people think eating fruits and vegetables is good for their health, but how many people actually know that that a cup of blueberries a week will actually reduce cognitive decline, specifically related to visual memory?” Villareal said. “We wanted to make this finding more real to people. How do we get more people to eat blueberries as easily as possible? Smoothies are very acceptable to people; they’re highly palatable.”
The findings support previous research that has shown that blueberries and the flavonoids they contain can slow aging and improve short-term memory loss. The researchers reported that their results were most consistent with the anthocyanins (a flavonoid) in blueberries.
Funding for the study came from the Agricultural Marketing Service of the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the National Institutes of Health.
Though the study found a link between blueberries and improved memory, further research is needed to confirm whether blueberries may be effective in preventing or reversing cognitive decline. Future studies could explore how other fruits and berries impact cognitive function, as well as how the same amount of blueberries, but in other formats (for example, in a cookie), might affect cognitive function, Villareal said.
Bottom Line:
If you are at risk for diabetes or memory loss, consider adding blueberries to your weekly smoothies. If you’d rather snack on the blueberries, try them in a salad or a yogurt parfait. Just be aware that the exact amount and frequency of blueberries may vary based on your individual health needs.

Lower Motor Neurons (LMN) disorders involve nerve cells that directly control the muscles of the body. A common example is Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig's disease. In the late 19th century, the development of electric lights transformed how people lit their homes and other buildings. Two of the most significant contributors to this development were British inventor Joseph Swan and American inventor Thomas Edison.

**Joseph Swan**

Joseph Wilson Swan (1828-1914) was an English physicist, chemist, and inventor. He is often considered one of the co-inventors of the incandescent light bulb, though his work in this field was influenced by similar efforts made by Thomas Edison. In 1878, Swan patented a design for an incandescent light bulb using a carbon fiber filament. This was one of the earliest known practical light bulbs, and Swan continued to refine his design over the following years. In 1880, he received a British patent for the improved design. By 1882, Swan had established the world's first central electricity generation and distribution company, supplying electricity and light to homes and businesses.

**Thomas Edison**

Thomas Alva Edison (1847-1931) was an American inventor and businessman. Known as the "Wizard of Menlo Park," he developed the first practical incandescent light bulb in 1879. Edison's design used a thicker, more durable carbon filament made from bamboo, which allowed the light bulb to burn brighter and for longer periods. Edison filed his patent application for the incandescent light bulb in October 1879, and it was granted in January 1880. Edison's approach to creating the incandescent light bulb was characterized by extensive testing and experimentation, which helped to identify the optimal materials for the filament.

**Their Research and Competition**

Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison were both working independently on the development of incandescent light bulbs around the same time, but Edison's patented invention was more durable and practical than Swan's earlier models. In 1880, Swan publicly demonstrated his electric light system in England, while Edison was also working on a similar system in the United States. 

The two inventors began negotiating with each other in the late 1880s, eventually reaching an agreement in January 1888. They decided to combine their patents and establish the Edison & Swan United Electric Light Company, which later became the General Electric Company in the United States. This collaboration allowed the two inventors to pool their resources and expertise, making their lightbulbs more efficient and reliable.

**Comparison of Their Work**

Although both Swan and Edison contributed to the development of practical incandescent light bulbs, there were some key differences in their approaches:

- Filament Material: Swan used a carbonized paper filament, while Edison developed a more durable and efficient bamboo-based filament.
- Focus: Swan concentrated on improving the durability of his bulbs and founding a lighting company, while Edison aimed to develop a complete electrical system, including power generation and distribution.
- Patents: Both inventors applied for patents for their lightbulb designs. Swan's original patents were granted in the UK and Italy, while Edison's were granted in the United States and Germany.

In conclusion, the invention of practical electric lights in the 19th century was a result of significant contributions from multiple inventors, including Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison. Despite their competition, they eventually collaborated to create a more durable and efficient light bulb that revolutionized the lighting industry.

The original coat of arms of Warsaw, like the seal, showed a sea monster in its original state of disrepair.
The Mermaid has always been associated with Warsaw. In 1588 King Sigismund III Vasa (the ruler of Poland and a descendant of the Jagiellonians (Jagiełlos)) married Sweden's Queen Sigrid (Zofia).  Wedding gifts from the Polish side included the maiden armor of Blanka Zbarawska, the 'Armia Syreny', which is believed to have been fashioned by the famous armorialist Walter Rymarz.  It was the Mermaid that was featured on the under armor. Not too long after this, paintings of the Polish Royal family began to show the son of Sigismund and Zofia holding the 'armed shield' of Blanka.  This tradition continued to the House of Czartoryski and the Mazovian Voivodes.  

No official symbol or civic seal had been designated for the city of Warsaw during this time.  The first such seal, commonly referred to as "Soltyk's seal", was the first seal to show the Mermaid and it was made around 1440. It consisted of a round seal bordered with the Latin inscription Sigilium Civitatis Varsoviensis (Seal of the city of Warsaw). However it did not come into use by the city until the 18th century when it became the first of the civic seals in use until 1945.
As Warsaw grew it needed an official civic seal.  The first was the result of the work of King Sigismund II Augustus (the grand-nephew of King Sigismund III Vasa) who had a civic seal of Warsaw engraved in 1565. It showed an oval seal bearing the Latin inscription Sigilium Municipalitatis Varsoviae (Seal of the civic authorities of Warsaw). It was made of lead and engraved by Maestro Vincenzio Genauro. Genauro was an Italian who had settled in Kraków (Korczak) in 1549.  It has been preserved in the history collections of the National Museum in Warsaw.
During the years 1816-1829 the mermaid, in the form we now know her, appears in the earliest known architecture. At the end of the 19th century, wall paintings bearing the image of the mermaid appeared in the Union Chamber (Polish: Kamerę Związkową, German: Unionkammer) and a murial decorated with a mermaid had been added to the building of the Club of the Officers of the Saxon Legion (Szkolna Słoneczna).
In 1945 the reality of the Red Army advancing into the country brought with it the Soviet Union.  The Communist Party replaced the Polish Government and a new currency was introduced, the Zloty.  Many of the original paintings and frescos in the city were destroyed. To eliminate reminders of the past, statues of King John III Sobieski were removed, and both the Royal Castle and the Saxon Garden were razed to the ground. The landmark, situated in Plac Bankowy (Bank Square) in the Old Town, of the birthplace of Stefan Czarniecki (the military commander of the Commonwealth of Poland-Lithuania) and the monument to Prince Jan Zamoyski were removed as well.
The communist government replaced the official civic seal of Warsaw with a star and compass rose. The image of the mermaid and other figures that made Warsaw a place of culture and heritage were replaced with images of the USSR's leader, Joseph Stalin, and the lyrics of the "Internationale", a communist anthem.
The seal of the communist city was in official use for over 20 years.  It was replaced in 1972 with the civic seal of the People's Republic of Poland.

From 1963 to 2005, BBC Video and BBC Books, and from 2005 to 2010, BBC Video alone, released Doctor Who programme videos and ancillary content on videotape. This began in 1963 with the release of "An Unearthly Child". This was initially limited to the serials but later extended to include audio commentaries and such features as "making-of" documentaries and individual episodes of the programme itself. In 2009, the entire collection of BBC-produced Doctor Who videotapes was released on DVD with exclusive bonus material and under the banner "Dr Who – Full Circle". From 2005 to 2010, all episodes of the revived series were released on DVD in sets of 8 or 12, followed by box sets containing 2 or 3 seasons. Starting with Series 4, the studio releases have received a mixed reception, although television broadcasts and audio releases have received widespread acclaim. The logo used for the earliest videotapes was an adaptation of the Tardis box on the television logo. The logo for the videotapes featured a logo of the Doctor Who logo with the text "Doctor Who" added below it in the font and colours from the television logo. 

The logo for the revived series videocassettes was a black TARDIS with a white "DW". Each season and episode had a different texture added to the TARDIS with different themes being followed per season. The colour of the "DW" changed with the Doctor. This logo was used until 2015. Starting in 2006 and continuing for the remainder of the 2000s, the series was released on DVD with exclusives which were not released in video. These were added to the releases in the late 2010s (starting with Series 8) as DVD releases were replaced with Blu-ray releases. From 2007 to 2015, the logo on DVD releases from BBC Video was updated and kept to the logo, which was used from 1999 to 2010 and also continued to be used in all of the DVD releases. Doctor Who is a British science fiction television programme produced by the BBC since 1963. The programme depicts the adventures of a Time Lord called the Doctor, an extraterrestrial being from the planet Gallifrey. He explores the universe in a time-travelling space ship called the TARDIS, accompanied by members of various species. The series was created by writer and producer Terrance Dicks and producer Verity Lambert for the BBC. The programme has broadcast continually since its first appearance on 23 November 1963, with just a few exceptions.

Daleks were originally conceived for the 1963 serial "The Daleks". Writer Terry Nation was asked to come up with a creature that was unlike any monster then on television, so that the Doctor could encounter it and that the audience would not have seen before. Nation drew on the look of the spectre of "death by suffocation", the respiratory apparatus of early respirators, a period drawing of a turtle with a fan cooling its shell, and inspiration from a Chinese dragon. Further development of the concept included designing the Dalek as an anthropomorphic tank and giving the actors control over the Dalek's "movements", even though they were immobile. The overall appearance of the first Daleks was modelled after the Skorzeny commandos, and each of the Daleks's three big vents were inspired by the shape of a likeness of television comedian Danny La Rue, sculpted on the model's tail by its designer, Philip Kindred. The Dalek's name has several possible origins, including the rhyming slang term "allacked", derived from "it never lays", and "nallack", a form of the Anglo-Saxon expression "not call back"; however, in 1996 Nation claimed the name was his and took all credit.

Pedagogy describes teaching methods. The term was first used by the Prussian educator Hermann Heinrich Graff in 1806 and was adopted by Johann Friedrich Herbart in 1809. Herbart, his supporters and their critics are often referred to respectively as 'orthodox', 'neo-orthodox' and 'progressive' pedagogists.
In its later version, pedagogy had a second, negative meaning, that of a didactic, authoritarian style of teaching. This style of teaching often refers to traditional, textbook-oriented classrooms with a student centered in a teacher. Many modern schools combine these two versions of the concept of pedagogy, discussing the combination of both good and bad teaching and the need for the pedagogical aspects of teaching to develop and be modified accordingly.
Generally the term 'pedagogy' today refers to a positive idea of teaching, one that offers the teaching profession the opportunity to examine and improve the complex area of education. It enables teachers to provide explanations of knowledge, skills and values in their classes. Pedagogy integrates research to offer teachers new skills to help students learn better.
Types of pedagogy
Teaching is used to transfer information, but is an imperfect method of information transfer. Direct, absolute teaching is fraught with difficulties, particularly in the English language, where a precise definition or a word that could define knowledge is difficult to find. This is one reason that there are numerous pedagogical philosophies and theories.

In the field of arts education, several different methods have been utilized by artistic disciplines (e.g. music education, dance education, drama education) for many centuries: these are often known as 'traditional', 'instrumental' or ' applied music lessons' or 'private' lessons. Many of these pedagogical philosophies can date back to the ideas and methods of several different cultural figures: Shinichi Suzuki, discoverer of the Suzuki method and his belief in the importance of music education; Joseph Callaway and Sanford A. Lewis, creators of the Orff Schulwerk and their ideas about the connection between music and movement and between different modalities of learning; Nadia Boulanger, renowned music teacher who taught and mentored many great composers, conductors and artists in her life; Sergei Rachmaninoff and Vladimir and Vlada Horowitz, for their performance and pedagogical philosophies, and many others. These methods were previously practiced in a private, one-on-one or small group atmosphere, although some of the methods are now practiced in public school, conservatory, and private studio settings.

Traditional teaching methods focused on rote learning or imitation of a teacher or master (see Socratic method). Many of these methods date back to a time when education was focused on the teaching of knowledge and skills in the liberal arts or for specific professions and trades, often with a reliance on oral or manual transmission of the master's knowledge or skill. For example, the role of early Greek and Roman teachers in the education of the elite was to teach 'how to learn'. For the Romans, the tutor's role in the home was also a mentor and role model whose guidance was thought essential for the proper socialization of the young. Teachers' roles in family and society were central to personal development and involved systematic, experiential learning within the context of the family.

In Europe in the post-Enlightenment period, several progressive and reformist pedagogical theories were developed by European educators, based on ideas such as a close study of child development (Jean-Jacques Rousseau), the application of psychology to pedagogy (Karl Groos, Wilhelm Wundt, W. K. McDougall, Edward Titchener and others), the breaking down of complex skills into smaller units (Johann Gruenberg), the elimination of a rote learning in favor of active learning (Paul strong suggestion and some other theories) and cooperation (Felix Adler) between students and teachers, the application of "scientific" theories in general to the classroom (John Dewey) and the importance of play in socialization (Erik Erikson and others). Some new educational practices (e.g., Friedrich Fröbel's "kindergarten") or traditional ones revivified by new focus (Jean Montessori's "unit block" play and practical life exercises) and in some instances came to dominate education; others (such as those of Montessori) were significantly restricted by major political changes (such as the rise of Fascism).

The Industrial Revolution in Great Britain and the subsequent strong economic growth there through the 19th and 20th centuries necessitated formal schooling for the entire population. Schools were organized around academic courses of study which, despite regular updates, primarily focused on rote memorization and passive, competitive, individualistic learning. Private tutoring and schools for the elite (such as Eton College in England and Phillips Exeter Academy in the United States) were exceptions. John Dewey, philosopher, psychologist and proponent of educational reform, advocated a different approach to education. He criticized what he considered a outdated and authoritarian mode of instruction by teachers, noting the focus on mere information transmission, the teaching of unimportant material and the abdication of active learning in the classroom, especially active learning with regard to moral values. He argued for the need to revise teaching methods and the purposes of schooling and education as a whole.

The British population numbered around 1,600,000 and was primarily concentrated in the 13 colonies along the Atlantic seaboard. They were mostly English, with important Irish and Scottish communities in the eastern cities. Many German settlements were located in Pennsylvania and the valley of the middle Susquehanna River. Most American colonists of British origin spoke English as their first language; there were significant minorities of Welsh speakers in south-eastern Pennsylvania, and French speakers in Quebec and southern Quebec-New Hampshire. Dutch speakers were found in the lower Hudson River Valley, once part of the Dutch colony of New Netherland. Swedes and small German groups of Lutherans settled in Delaware. Significant minority groups across the colonies included free people of color and slaves. Colonial laws differentiated between free white males (of English origin) and men of all other backgrounds, including women and free people of color. Native Americans were considered "enemies without a nation", and not full members of any nation, under the law.
The French colonies under royal control were governed by a governor, typically of captain's rank, who had most of the civil and judicial powers but had to answer to the French Ministry of Marine. New France had an Estates General, like France itself, consisting of representatives of the Church, nobility, and Third Estate (commoners), though its powers were quite limited. French settlement was sparse, limited to a few outposts at ports, river crossings, and mines. Most French were concentrated to the St. Lawrence settlement, with a small outpost at Mobile Bay, in the Caribbean (present-day Haiti), and scattered fur traders and trappers along the Hudson, Ohio, Mississippi and Missouri Rivers. The French were heavily dependent on an alliance with First Nations, particularly the Ojibwa, Ottawa and Huron. They fought many wars with their Indian allies against the Iroquois Confederacy, whose lands lay between New France and the British colonies.
The English colonies were very diverse. The 13 colonies along the Atlantic coast were primarily governed by a governor appointed by the king, under civil and judicial laws established by a locally elected legislative assembly. The Carolinas were divided into North and South in 1712. There was a Supreme Court of Trade in London which regulated the colonies' trade. In 1683, William Penn created Pennsylvania with a charter that granted equal rights to all inhabitants. In most colonies, the majority of the population was English; however, there were areas which were settled by Dutch, Irish, and Germans. German and Scots-Irish immigrants began settling in the backcountry near the Appalachian Mountains, outside the control of local authorities. As frontiersmen, they clashed frequently with the French and their Indian allies. Each side was also allied with various regional Indian tribes that became increasingly involved in the conflicts. After the Iroquois were defeated in the French and Indian War, settlers quickly moved onto their land in upstate New York and in the upper Ohio River Valley.
In the northern and middle colonies, the population grew rapidly from natural increase. In Virginia and other southern colonies, growth was mostly from immigration. Some immigrants came as indentured servants, typically poor people who served several years, cleared land, and became citizens. Other immigrants were brought as slaves from Africa, mostly from the west coast of Africa. Most slaves worked as field hands in agriculture. Though European colonists lived in fear of Indian attacks for decades after the end of the French and Indian War, in reality the danger was minor. In most areas, the Indian tribes were too poor and weakened to threaten the colonists. However, warfare between rival Indian tribes was common, and Indians attacked European settlements.

Establishing an international order, especially after an international crisis, is complex and hard-won.
The post-COVID19 period is fraught with uncertainty and rapidly shifting global realities. It is also fraught with opportunity. To seize this moment, leaders need to summon their strategic thinking and act in a cooperative manner on a wide range of issues – fighting the virus, lifting livelihoods, deploying COVID-19 vaccines, reconstituting economies, and of course stabilizing the international environment. For some, the most pressing task is to ensure that the spectre of another great-power war does not reemerge on the international horizon.
Many world leaders have announced ambitious multilateral visions since 2019. In September 2019, President Xi Jinping, for example, defined a China-led system of multilateralism “for a community with a shared future for mankind.” Building such a community, he said, is predicated on achieving multilateralism with Chinese characteristics, not least by safeguarding global security in areas such as information security and “cyberspace security” and by ensuring that the existing world order is maintained. The US has no shortage of rhetoric on that front, either. Speaking at the same event, President Donald J. Trump outlined his blueprint for “a Free and Open Indo-Pacific” and said it would be “built on free and fair trade, equal access to resources and markets, and an inclusive approach that benefits all nations.” On other issues – such as seeking to ban end-to-end encryption or rejecting the recent World Health Organization reform proposals – US and Chinese actions have been increasingly divergent. However, in others – such as negotiating a trade agreement and, to a certain extent, cooperating on issues related to the pandemic – the two major powers are increasingly working together.
Such an environment of tit-for-tat actions, which is often described as “cooperation” in some quarters, would hardly make multilateralism work. Indeed, it tends to reduce the shared global outlook among nations to a set of rival collective goals that sets nations against each other. It is not clear where these large-scale cooperation agreements will take the world. Rather, this kind of bidding war results in a very weak multilateral system, if not a moribund one.
Efforts to set and rebuild the global order are not new. A World Economic Forum workshop will bring together prominent international leaders and multilateral policymakers from six regions of the world. This workshop aims to reframe the notions of cooperation and multilateralism. In an era of extreme domestic polarization, where the leaders of the global powerhouses no longer have the room to maneuver as they previously did, what roles will multilateral institutions play? How will leaders respond to the structural changes in the global order, the impact of the pandemic and the climate crisis? Is it possible to build a new global order that reflects the emerging world and achieves the multilateral order envisioned by the post-war architects?

By the 1890s many railway companies had adopted the more reliable superheated steam as the preferred means of heat transfer in their locomotives. This was because it enabled steam locomotives to use faster combustion temperatures as the fuel was not allowed to mix with air until the burnt gases entered the boilers proper, where they were still at 400 °F. The drawback of superheating was that it required redesign of conventional steam valves, which were generally replaced with dynamic valves. These latter valves were cut out or inset into the valve gears, which were sprung with adjustable helical springs to maximize the valve's cone angle as was shown by the Crookes valve gear company during the 1880s. Dynamic valves' main operating difference is that they open earlier in their cycle than normally constructed "standard" slide valves. This is because dynamic valves open using a conical sliding action, with their base canted at a particular angle. Standard slide valves open in a far more linear manner. This simple change dramatically increased the speed and volume of air entering the boiler, reducing the ignition time and ensuring a far more constant boiler temperature and higher overall pressure. In Britain the fitting of dynamic valves was first experimented with on the Cornwall Railway in the late 1860s, but the first commercial introduction occurred on the Grand Trunk Railway in Canada, where it was pioneered by John Bryden, an engineer who had worked for Sir Henry Brunel's Peninsular and Oporto Railway. At the time, the introduction of his design caused the GTR to purchase a number of Doncaster locomotives.
Dynamic valves did not gain wide acceptance in the UK and European rail industries until around the late 1910s, after years of proving themselves in the hands of British designers. Many locomotives used today by various United Kingdom narrow gauge railways possess dynamic valves. The United States quickly adopted the new technology, and it remains in use there to this day. The Canadian Railroad Museum in Ottawa is home to the example below, a pair of Walschaerts-Dynamic rotary steam valve gears fitted to an 0-6-0 tender locomotive built by the Montreal Locomotive Works for the Grand Trunk.
