Steam engines frequently possess two independent mechanisms for ensuring that the pressure in the boiler does not go too high; one may be adjusted by the user, the second is typically designed as an ultimate fail-safe. Such safety valves traditionally used a simple lever to restrain a plug valve in the top of a boiler. One end of the lever carried a weight or spring that restrained the valve against steam pressure. Early valves could be adjusted by engine drivers, leading to many accidents when a driver fastened the valve down to allow greater steam pressure and more power from the engine. The more recent type of safety valve uses an adjustable spring-loaded valve, which is locked such that operators may not tamper with its adjustment unless a seal illegally is broken. This arrangement is considerably safer.[citation needed]
By the 1890s many railway companies had adopted the more reliable superheated steam as the preferred means of heat transfer in their locomotives. This was because it enabled steam locomotives to use faster combustion temperatures as the fuel was not allowed to mix with air until the burnt gases entered the boilers proper, where they were still at 400 °F. The drawback of superheating was that it required redesign of conventional steam valves, which were generally replaced with dynamic valves. These latter valves were cut out or inset into the valve gears, which were sprung with adjustable helical springs to maximize the valve’s cone angle as was shown by the Crookes valve gear company during the 1880s. These changes came about as steam locomotive engineers sought to improve the temperature differential on the boilers internal superheaters. Steam locomotive valve gears were soon redesigned to cope with the increased inlet pressures.
Dynamic valves’ main operating difference is that they open earlier in their cycle than normally constructed “standard” slide valves. This is because dynamic valves open using a conical sliding action, with their base canted at a particular angle. Standard slide valves open in a far more linear manner. This simple change dramatically increased the speed and volume of air entering the boiler, reducing the ignition time and ensuring a far more constant boiler temperature and higher overall pressure. In Britain the fitting of dynamic valves was first experimented with on the Cornwall Railway in the late 1860s, but the first commercial introduction occurred on the Grand Trunk Railway in Canada, where it was pioneered by John Bryden, an engineer who had worked for Sir Henry Brunel’s Peninsular and Oporto Railway. At the time, the introduction of his design caused the GTR to purchase a number of Doncaster locomotives.
Dynamic valves did not gain wide acceptance in the UK and European rail industries until around the late 1910s, after years of proving themselves in the hands of British designers. Many locomotives used today by various United Kingdom narrow gauge railways possess dynamic valves. The United States quickly adopted the new technology, and it remains in use there to this day. The Canadian Railroad Museum in Ottawa is home to the example below, a pair of Walschaerts-Dynamic rotary steam valve gears fitted to an 0-6-0 tender locomotive built by the Montreal Locomotive Works for the Grand Trunk. Both valve gears were “aftermarket” items as the locomotive was initially built by the Montreal firm, and then sold to the Grand Trunk in 1879, at which time it was fitted with Walschaerts-Dynamic gears.

List out the structure of an organism
An organism is a living, self-sustaining entity that comprises one or more cells and exhibits life functions such as growth, metabolism, reproduction, and responding to external stimuli. The structural organization of an organism can vary greatly depending on its complexity, size, and type. However, most organisms can be broadly categorized into four major levels of biological organization: cells, tissues, organs, and organ systems. 

1. Cells: Cells are the basic building blocks of all living organisms, consisting of a membrane-bound compartment containing various cellular components and structures such as the nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, and cytoplasm. Single-celled organisms, like bacteria and protozoa, are the simplest form of life, while multicellular organisms are made up of trillions of specialized cells.

2. Tissues: Tissues are groups of similar cells that work together to perform a specific function. There are four types of tissues in animal organisms: epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissues. Each tissue type is composed of different cell types specialized for particular roles, such as providing protection, supporting structures, generating movement, or transmitting signals.

3. Organs: Organs are formed by the aggregation of different tissues that work together to accomplish a specific task. Examples of organs include the heart, lungs, liver, and brain. These structures are designed to carry out specific physiological functions, such as pumping blood, exchanging gases, detoxification, or controlling and processing information.

4. Organ Systems: Organ systems are organized clusters of organs that function together to perform complex life activities. Major organ systems include the circulatory, respiratory, digestive, excretory, reproductive, and nervous systems. Each of these systems is essential for sustaining life and maintaining homeostasis.

Organisms can be classified based on their level of organization, including unicellular, multicellular, and eukaryotic. Eukaryotic cells are characterized by the presence of a true nucleus and organelles, whereas prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, lack these structures. Based on the number of cells and organization, organisms can be further divided into categories such as bacteria, archaea, fungi, plants, and animals.

what is photosynthesis
Photosynthesis is the biological process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria convert sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into glucose, a simple sugar, and oxygen. This process is crucial to life on Earth as it provides the primary energy source for almost all organisms and releases oxygen into the atmosphere, which is vital for the survival of aerobic organisms, including humans.

Photosynthesis occurs in two main stages: the light-dependent reactions and the light-independent reactions (also called the Calvin cycle). During the light-dependent reactions, pigments within photosynthetic organisms, like chlorophyll, capture light energy and use it to convert water molecules into oxygen and high-energy electrons. These electrons are used to create ATP (adenosine triphosphate), an energy-rich molecule that plants, algae, and some bacteria use to power the processes necessary for growth and metabolism.

The light-independent reactions, or the Calvin cycle, take place in the chloroplasts of plants and other photosynthetic organisms. In this stage, plants use ATP and the electrons from light-dependent reactions to convert carbon dioxide into glucose, which the plant can use for energy, growth, and reproduction. The glucose can also be stored in the plant for later use.

In summary, photosynthesis is a critical process that allows living organisms to convert sunlight into chemical energy, which is then used to sustain life and produce oxygen as a byproduct. It serves as the foundation of most ecosystems and plays a crucial role in maintaining the balance of life on Earth.

Brass instruments are musical instruments that rely solely or primarily on the player's lip muscles (lip vibrations) to produce sound. These instruments usually produce a buzzing sensation in the player's lower or upper lip, which in turn causes the air column to vibrate. This includes the trumpet, trombone, and tuba (which derive their sound primarily in this way) as well as the cornet, flugelhorn, French horn, mellophone, sousaphone, and various large and small bore bugles. Using the mouthpiece of each instrument alone (without the entire body of the instrument), one can produce buzzing sounds by directing air between the vibrating lips. In the case of the traditional trombone, the bore is straight, so the basic design of the instrument is that of a brass instrument. The tuba and sousaphone include serpentine and wrap tubing that extend the length of the instrument for comfort and practicality. The French horn uses coiled tubing, while the flute family can also be considered to use the "buzzing lips" technique, although a foot valve or lever is sometimes needed.
As with most brass instruments, some of the notes generated by buzzing the lips are out of tune for the purpose of establishing just intonation. To compensate, valves are used to lengthen and shorten the path of the vibrating air column. On tubas, French horns, and sousaphones, a single slide often provides enough length changes to alter a range of notes into a harmonious group, but smaller, more maneuverable trumpets, bugles, and some smaller tubas use valves. The cornet, mellophone and flugelhorn are similar, except that these instruments use no slides. Valves were not originally used with brass instruments because they change the acoustic length of the vibrating air column, which is especially noticeable at the lower end of the instrument. Historically, there was a very strong local grammar school tradition in Newcastle, with pupils taking scholarships exams and preparing for university in Year 9. After many years of decline, Newcastle City Council now only has two remaining grammar schools, both in Jesmond: Benfield School and St. Cuthbert's High School. Both are now all-girls schools. The third former grammar school to survive the abolition was Gosforth High School. However, it was rebranded as a university technical college in 2013, and so no longer part of the grammar school tradition. The government-funded charity New Schools Network is currently developing a new generation of academies for the city with the potential to provide more places for grammar school places in the city centre should a government at a future date choose to reverse the abolition of the tradition. Newcastle United Football Club is considered the city's de facto top team, having been one of Europe's leading clubs in the 1960s and the 1970s. They have won two European Cup/WC Fairs Cup Winners' Cups as well as the 1969 Fairs Cup/Super Cup and the 2010–11 UEFA Europa League. In addition, they have also been league champions a record 12 times, including a league and FA Cup "double" in 1969, and reached the FA Cup final a further six times. Both of these records are bettered only by Manchester United.
Sunderland are also considered Newcastle's main rivals, with the derby being termed the "Toon Togs". Sunderland, along with Newcastle United and Middlesbrough, have achieved promotion from the third tier of English football (the third division) in the last five seasons. Against Manchester United, Newcastle have managed three draws, two wins and two losses in five matches. The match between the two sides at St James' Park, on 20 December 2006, ended in an infamous brawl.
Newcastle United are one of only six clubs in the Premier League that have qualified for the UEFA Champions League in every season since it expanded from 12 clubs to 25 in 1996 (the other five are Arsenal, Chelsea, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur), and Newcastle United is one of only two teams in England (along with Manchester United) to have competed in European competition (including the FA Cup and Cup Winners' Cup) in every season since the second half of the 1969–70 season (having been relegated to the Third Division at the end of the first half of the 1968–69 season, with having been relegated from the First Division prior to that).

Historically, the River Tyne, also known as the Tine, flowed through the low-lying land of Northumberland and into the North Sea, through a broad inlet called the Firth of Tyne. In the Bronze Age, Newcastle was inhabited by the Ordovices, a British tribe of the same name, and contained a wooden crannog in Ouseburn. The settlement was later taken over by the Romans who developed it into a major port. It was at this time that the Castle Keep was built as the town's first fortification. It was known as Pons Aelius, meaning "Aelius' Bridge", after Emperor Hadrian, who ordered its construction in 122 CE during his visit to the province of Britain. The term "Stone Age" is a quaternary chronostratigraphic unit, and the corresponding technical name for its tools and artifacts is microlith. While the period roughly corresponds to the Paleolithic, Mesolithic, and Neolithic eras, many widely different cultures exist during each period, with regional variations. The Stone Age also spans cultural periods that are completely separated by long stretches of time. For example, the Neanderthals in Europe were replaced by anatomically modern humans carrying microlithic tool kits around 40,000 years BP, with no cultural continuity between the two populations.
In Great Britain the term is mainly applied to the prehistoric Stone Age, for which no writing exists, divided into three main periods: the Paleolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic.
In 2013 the Borehole Stratigraphy of the British Isles Project was launched with the aim of defining a standard stratigraphic column for Britain. Geological reconnaissance of the British Isles in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries was undertaken by a number of geologists, most of whom used the "impressive record of the Palaeolithic" (Blue clay, Oakham limestone and Bisle sand) as a stratigraphic marker.
Through this work, the British Isles were divided into a number of different stratigraphic basins, including the Thames, Solent, Pembrokeshire, Channel, Central Irish, Central English, Yorkshire, Irish Sea, Northern Irish and Moray basins. Each basin had a unique stratigraphic record and chronology based on the geologic information available at the time.
The three main cultural divisions of the Stone Age are defined for the British Isles as follows:
1. Early Stone Age - Paleolithic (began about 1.5 mya)
2. Late Stone Age - Mesolithic (4000 years bp)
3. Transitional Stone Age - Neolithic (8000 years bp)

1. Browse through the Library of Congress into the two document collections that contain the above book. The books themselves are written by Cambridge University Press and the Internet Archive. 2. Select the PDF files from this library that you want to make into HTML. For example, if you want to convert the [first volume](https://www.loc.gov/item/2006696422/), go to the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/volume1_d1_1937_to_1952unified_text) and select all the PDF files that have .txt in them. A rule of thumb to differentiate between the two document collections, as far as I can tell, is whether the document has "unified" in its filename (i.e. [this document](https://www.loc.gov/item/2006696422/) is from the Internet Archive and [this document](https://www.loc.gov/item/v1-vol17/), which doesn't have unified in its name, is from the Library of Congress).
3. Use the [OpenRefine](https://github.com/OpenRefine) tool to simplify the text and table of contents. This can be done by opening the PDF file in the tool, and then selecting all of the text and table of contents. This can be done by right-clicking on the text and selecting "Copy to the clipboard", and then pasting it into the tool.
4. Use the [Zettlekasten](https://github.com/zettlekasten/zettlekasten) tool to generate the HTML file. This can be done by opening the Zettlekasten tool and selecting the table of contents and text that was copied from the PDF file. This will generate the HTML file.
5. Save the HTML file as a .txt file and upload it to the [Open Philanthropy Project](https://www.openphilanthropy.org/giving/2005-books). This will make the data more easily accessible to the public.

    # Define a function to analyze the interaction between entities

    # Reformat the article based on the specified entities
    reformatted_article = '\n'.join([
        rephrase_paragraph(para, entity) if entity in para else para for para in paragraphs

    # Summarize the interactions between the entities

    return final_response

It is a complex eating disorder with serious physical, psychological, and social consequences. It is not always associated with any obvious cause, although sometimes it may be associated with underlying conditions such as substance abuse and depression. Anorexia nervosa is associated with increased risk for suicide and even death. Anorexia is often mistaken for other medical conditions, such as cancer or anemia, because it can cause similar symptoms; however, these conditions can be ruled out with medical tests. The diagnosis of anorexia can then be made based on a careful history of weight loss, low body mass index, and a fear of gaining weight. Physical complications can arise from weight loss or malnutrition (insufficient calorie intake) or overexertion leading to heart failure. Some families have been known to foster an "over-competitive atmosphere" where parents encourage their children to excel in every aspect of life—including academics, sports, social skills and emotional well-being. Immunodeficiency is any deficiency in the immune system's ability to fight infectious disease or cancer. Immunodeficiency can either be congenital (present at birth) or acquired ("secondary") following the transmission of viruses or other infectious agents (see immunodeficiency).
Immunodeficiencies can also be induced by medications or other diseases. Treatment is dependent on the type of immunodeficiency present. If the underlying cause of the immunodeficiency can be removed or corrected, the immune system may be able to return to a normal state. Otherwise, drugs such as immunoglobulin replacement, antibiotics, and bone marrow transplantation may be used to help prevent or treat complications.
The immune system is defined as a collection of mechanisms within an organism that protects against disease by identifying and killing pathogens or other potentially harmful foreign bodies. These mechanisms include the production of specific antibodies by B cells and lymphocyte activation. Immunodeficiency may therefore be manifested as a lack of specific antibodies (as in B cell deficiency) or lymphopenia (as in T cell deficiency). Immunodeficiency has also been found to influence cancer, as the immune system can act as a tumor suppressor, and immunosuppression may lead to an increased risk of cancer development.
Immune response consists of both specific and nonspecific immune systems. The specific immune system is further subdivided into innate immunity and adaptive immunity. The innate immunity refers to non-specific immune components, for example, physical barriers such as skin, chemical barriers (digestive enzymes, for example) and blood-brain barrier. The adaptive immunity refers to the 'specific' immune components, for example, Antigen-presenting cells (APCs), T and B lymphocytes, B cell memory, and so on.
The way a specific immunodeficiency is caused depends on which part of the immune system is defective. Antibody deficiency disorders may be caused by defective B cells or T cells. They may also be the result of defects in other cells or proteins needed for the production of antibodies. In some cases, the cause of antibody deficiency disorder is an inherited abnormality. In other cases, it is acquired. For example, HIV infection leads to progressive B cell defect and antibody deficiency.
Usually, immunodeficiencies manifest as recurrent bacterial and fungal infections and autoimmune manifestations. Complications due to chronic autoimmune phenomena such as SLE may also occur in immunodeficiencies.
Cancers can also cause immunodeficiency. They might be the result of genetic disorders such as BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations in hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. Chromosomal abnormalities such as in T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) may also lead to defects in the immune system.
This includes a spectrum of disorders ranging from the most severe ones that have early-onset and lead to progressive morbidity and early death, to milder conditions that are evident only after birth or during early childhood.
In the context of immunodeficiency, prophylactic use of antibiotics is sometimes required to prevent infections. Infection prevention by vaccination and avoiding contact with those who are sick or infected are also some of the protective methods commonly used in those with primary immunodeficiencies.
Different studies describe different findings with regards to cancer incidence in patients with immunodeficiency. Several cancers have been found to be more common than in the general population, including leukemias and lymphomas, and solid cancers such as melanoma, lip cancer, breast cancer, colon cancer, rectal cancer, and non-gastric lymphoma. In other patients, cancer incidence is equivalent to that seen in healthy individuals.

## The Psychology of Mother-Child Relationship
According to "The Psychoanalytical Study of the Child", by Anna Freud, three phases exist during the mother-child relationship—
## The Ullus Phase (0–4 months): The Mother as a Ullus
Ullus means a container in Latin. In this phase, the child associates his/her mother with the feeling of fullness, which he/she receives through the breasts. During this phase, the child perceives the mother as a container who will always be able to provide and take away the feeling of fullness. This is also called the 'Breast as Ullus' phase.
## The Anal Phase (4 months – 2 years): Mother as an Object
During this phase, the child develops an ability to distinguish between himself/herself and the mother. While the sense of identification between the mother and the child still exists, they start to see themselves as separate entities. This phase ends when the child can speak, with the use of specific words.

### Transition from the Anal Stage to the phallic stage

In the phallic stage, the child is occupied with gender identification and sexual fixation.   
## The Phallic Stage (2 years – 5 years):The Mother as a Member of an institution
The child now recognizes the gender of his/her mother. The child's sexual wishes, in terms of his/her mother, are split. The boy child then develops castration anxiety, which results in the fixation of a superego. The girl child develops the Electra complex and starts to develop interests in her future husband and the desires of her mother.
As mentioned above, the child's perceptions towards their mother vary significantly throughout their life. It is during the phallic stage that we see the association of mother with negative attributes in the child's mind.

def analyze_article(title, text, entities):
    rephrased_texts = [text]
    for entity in entities:
        new_text = rephrased_texts[-1].replace(entity, f"*{entity}*")

    sorted_indices = sorted(interaction_entity_indices)
    for i, idx in enumerate(sorted_indices[:-1]):
        if idx + len(entities[i]) < sorted_indices[i + 1]:
            interaction = rephrased_texts[i][idx:idx + len(entities[i + 1])]

### Discussion of Geology in relation to Paleozoic
The Paleozoic era was a time of great significance in the history of life on Earth. It was characterized by the evolution of many key groups of organisms, including fish, amphibians, reptiles, and early forms of insects. This era saw the emergence of the first true land plants and the diversification of marine ecosystems. It was also marked by several mass extinction events, which had profound effects on the composition of life on our planet. 

### Discussion of Geology in relation to Epoch
The concept of an epoch is essential in understanding the geological time scale. An epoch is a subdivision of a period, and it represents a significant period of geological history during which certain events or changes took place. For example, the Quaternary period, which encompasses the last two and a half million years, includes two epochs: the Pleistocene and the Holocene. Each epoch has its own unique characteristics and features, such as distinct climatic conditions, geological processes, and biological evolution. Understanding these epochs helps us better comprehend the complex history of our planet and its inhabitants.

The interaction between the Paleozoic era and the concept of an epoch is multifaceted and crucial for understanding the broader context of Earth's geological history. The Paleozoic era marks the beginning of extensive and significant geological changes on our planet, setting the stage for many evolutionary milestones that define the history of life. Epochs within the Paleozoic period, such as the Cambrian and the Permian, represent smaller segments of this larger era during which specific geological processes and biological developments occurred. By breaking down the Paleozoic era into epochs, geologists can analyze and document the progression of events more systematically, providing insights into the complex interplay between Earth's physical environment and the evolving ecosystems it supports. In geology, an epoch is a subdivision of the geologic timescale that is smaller than a period and larger than an age. Epochs are most often named after a distinctive rock stratum that occurs worldwide ("lithostratigraphic markers") or a significant evolutionary change in life. For example, the Cretaceous epoch saw the rise of angiosperms and the dominance of dinosaurs.

### Discussion of Geology in relation to Era
An era is a division of geologic time longer than an epoch and shorter than a period. Eras are divided into sub-eras, and they are distinguished by major changes in Earth's geological history such as mass extinctions or glaciations. Notable eras include the Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic eras.

This hierarchical relationship allows geologists to study and understand the intricate history of Earth in greater detail.

John Wesley was born on 2 February 1703 in Epworth, Lincolnshire, England. He was educated at Charterhouse School, Westminster School and Oxford University. After graduating from Oxford, Wesley became a priest in the Church of England. He had six younger brothers, two of whom also became prominent clergymen.
During the eighteenth century, Wesley and his younger brother Charles Wesley (1707-88), a poet, were at the centre of the Methodist revival. A tour of the English mining industry highlighted the 'destitute, lonely, comfortless state of so many poor sinners' and also the absence of priests. John and Charles published their Sermons in 1739-40 and in 1738 experienced salvation after hearing a reading from the New Testament Book of Romans.
From 1739 John Wesley began preaching across the country, alone and with his brother. He presented a message of salvation to an increasingly desperate urban population. His sermons focused on the sincerity of individual repentance, and then received the Holy Spirit (an experience Wesley described as an 'ardent sense of pardoning grace and love'). These experiences also gave Wesley a theology of faith and works, with a stress on human agency, especially regarding how to combat sin.
The eighteenth century witnessed dramatic changes in London society. Wealthy industrialists resided in large homes along the Thames and other rivers, while workers remained 'on the streets', exposed to poverty, sin and immorality. Reformers such as John Wesley, along with leaders such as William Wilberforce and Thomas Clarkson, agitated to reduce the number of destitute people in Britain.
Workhouse records show that around 670,000 people were treated in workhouses in 1834, compared with 421,000 people in 1825. In 1806 the population in London was 1.1 million. By 1839 it was more than 2 million. In 1750, 20 percent of Londoners lived in slums. This figure rose to 70 percent in 1839. Although many workers died young due to intense poverty, the number of individuals aged under 30 years in London increased from 398,000 in 1825 to 420,000 in 1834. This meant that the number of workers in the 10-to-19-year age group in London increased from 172,000 in 1825 to 266,000 in 1834.
London slums were large concentrations of working class people living in tiny dwellings. Slums offered no toilets or running water, and inadequate sanitation. People also suffered from hunger, violence, lack of medical care and the use of immoral language in many circumstances. Morality was described as an element of the Protestant religion, specifically the Church of England, which ministered to the spiritual needs of Londoners.
At one workhouse in Horsham, Hants, a worker at the department responsible for organising poor relief in 1835 wrote:
And thus it often happens, that the mendicant, when he cannot live in respectable society, because the fear of being identified with a 'squire' or a banker is of a lower order than that which prevents him from cohabiting with his mistress, invades the slums, where he is driven by the force of starvation.

title: Steam engine
context: The first commercially successful true engine, in that it could generate power and transmit it to a machine, was the atmospheric engine, invented by Thomas Newcomen around 1712. It was an improvement over Savery's steam pump, using a piston as proposed by Papin. Newcomen's engine was relatively inefficient, and in most cases was used for pumping water. It worked by creating a partial vacuum by condensing steam under a piston within a cylinder. It was employed for draining mine workings at depths hitherto impossible, and also for providing a reusable water supply for driving waterwheels at factories sited away from a suitable "head". Water that had passed over the wheel was pumped back up into a storage reservoir above the wheel.

Willard says of this device:
... thus, by applying steam to a vacuum it was made for the first time in the history of the world, possible to derive mechanical force, not from the power of falling water, or the contraction of fire upon an enclosed fluid, but from the heat of the sun, everywhere uniformly diffused, and at the ordinary temperature of the atmosphere capable of producing an atmospheric pressure of more than fifteen pounds upon every square inch. Willard predicted "that future ages would regard this discovery as more momentous than that of [Newton's] system of gravitation or of any other event of which history has preserved the remembrance as connected with the human race."
James Watt did not come up with the concept of a steam engine. The credit for the invention of the steam engine with a separate condenser chamber goes to Thomas Savery, who filed his design with the English government in 1698. Joseph Jenner published his design for a steam engine in 1698; Savery wrote in response, saying, "This is not new, but old as the Times." Savery's engine resembled the hammer engine of Hero of Alexandria in 60 A.D. and resembled Blaugius's engine in 100 A.D. Unlike the Hero, Savery's engine used either low or high-pressure steam and pumps the water out.
The invention of the steam engine is regarded as a milestone that helped drive the Industrial Revolution. It also dramatically increased mining production and the development of some of the earliest factories. Because steam engines could be powered by coal or wood in areas with few energy sources, they allowed for the Industrial Revolution to occur in the United Kingdom. In 1792, with an increase in engine size, it was calculated that a Watt steam engine could deliver a water pump 4 to 6 horsepower. Early in the 19th century, the output of a single engine had reached 600 horsepower. Their efficiency eventually reached 30%.
Evidence of the first steam engine built in Ottoman Turkey is the remains of an existing steam-powered machine built by the Ottoman prince Mihri Sucessor of Sultan Ahmed III, in 1754 which is currently on display in the Topkapi Palace. The machine is called tel grafi (telegram machine) and has a wooden boiler, steam chest, wooden governor (incomplete), drip-pump mechanism, wooden framework, and it uses steam pressure of 5 psi. The scale of construction and theory of steam engine construction is also recorded on the Ottoman paper archive. Cybernetics:
Cybernetics is a scientific field that studies systems that receive feedback from the environment in which they operate, based on a comparison between the desired goal state and the current state, and the input/output relationships that exist between the two states. In an extended sense, a feedback system can be a device, an organism, a machine, a human organization, or a computational system in general, that uses information to govern its behavior, by determining what actions it must make to achieve an intended goal. The term "cybernetics" was popularized by Norbert Wiener in his book of 1948 with the intent to alert and inform the public about the common problems occurring in many of the "control and communication systems," and to address the need to find precise solutions to these common problems.
The term was coined by Norbert Wiener and appears in his first book in 1948, in "Cybernetics: or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine." He uses it to describe "Circular Causal and Feedback Mechanisms in Biological and Social Systems."  According to Wiener, cybernetics is to be distinguished from the word automaton: "An automaton is a quite special and specific kind of cybernetic machine (a machine which controls a process to achieve a goal) in which the function is prestabilized by another machine (in general a computing machine) in such a manner that the process is from that point on entirely mechanized, in a sense to be explained."
In a well-known introduction to the field, Wiener later elaborated,
In this sense, cybernetics is a rational formalism for the concept of "reflective" self-regulating systems. For example, a B-2 stealth airplane has sensors (eyes, etc.) to determine where it is relative to its goals (points A and B, etc.), and uses this information to self-correct its behavior to get closer to the desired goal. The sensors update the information, which can change the goal (because the plane may receive new instructions during flight). This continuous feedback between process, information, and goal are the basic principles of the field.
The word "cybernetic" derives from the Greek κυβερνήτης (kybernḗtēs), meaning "steersman, governor, rudder, helmsman".[a] It comes from a root meaning to govern.
'  This use of the word in biology is a continuation of the use of the word in Plato's dialogue Timaeus, where the term refers to the art of statesmanship in its ability to steer the state to an end, cf. Eirnster, 1941. Plato borrows the term from an Egyptian legend, which depicts a group of steersmen competing against one another for superiority in 'cybernêse'. They are, in turn, being guided by god Amun, the supreme guide (Isaak, 1945). Plato goes on to say that a "second analogy will illustrate the government of cities", namely the "relation between a pilot and his ship". The ship is a microcosm of the city, with the pilot controlling the correct combination of wind and ship to steer a path towards the desired goal, e.g., the city's best interests (Plato, 1970, p. 291d).
In a 1945 paper, Norbert Wiener, coined the term, describing it as "... concerned primarily with regulatory processes of all kinds and the simplest examples of such processes will, in fact, be found in the nonliving world" (Wiener, 1945).
Norbert Wiener proposed a correspondence with Constantin Carathéodory, during the late 1940s, but such a correspondence never happened. Instead, in the Greek-Polish period of his travels, Wiener sent his manuscript to Carathéodory, as he used the pseudonym of his American friend, P. S. Houtsma in order to get Carathéodory's approval. They discussed the manuscript, but didn't agree on the name chosen by Wiener. Carathéodory, who had defined the concept of a mathematical equivalent of a constructible program, claimed that 'Cybernetics' conveys the opposite meaning, as he noted that 'cybernetics' means autonomy, self-governance. They met in London, in 1950, where they held a five-day discussion over a coffee shop. Wiener agreed to change the name from 'Cybernetics' to 'Systems Theory', as he wanted to express a connection with the French term of 'La Cybernétique'. The name was also suggested by Carathéodory, referring to the relation with 'La Cybernétique', with the purpose of "avoiding misinterpretations" of the work being done in the field and to better explain what is understood by the term 'Cybernetics'. In 1953 Maududi founded a semi-monthly journal as the organ of the Jamaat. The journal's English language title was Islamic Studies. In its first issue, the editors stated:
> The ideal is to present, to the different divisions of the Islamic world, the teaching of Islam in their fullness, their nobility and their practicality ... We aim to present the world’s [sic] [i.e. the Islamic world's] requirement of a time-honoured truth. Here and there such a truth meets the resistance of vested interests but we shall strive to crush such resistance with relentless efforts and irresistible weapons. If this work is of any assistance to those interested in the propagation of Islam and its revival as a world force, it shall be rewarded abundantly. This work will assist them more effectively if it makes an impact on the intelligentsia and the so-called educated people of the countries belonging to the Islamic world. In the end our efforts will not be in vain.[3]

Maududi was a prolific author: he published hundreds of books and pamphlets, and many thousands of newspaper and journal articles.
Maududi's Islamic life is intertwined with the political life of Pakistan: from its formation in 1947 until his death, he was closely associated with the Jamaat-e-Islami, an organization which advocated a form of state which Maududi felt was consistent with the Islamic faith. He defined such a state as an Islamic state, which he felt should be politically Muslim and should ensure that the entire social and political order was governed by the Qur'an and the Sunnah.
One of Maududi's books, the "Brown February", was a strong attack on the international relations of colonial era India, especially the relations between Britain and India. It was a central text for the Jamiat ul-Ulema-e-Hind, a large collective of conservatives in India at the time. The Jamiat ul-Ulema-e-Hind sent a joint delegation to London, where it met with Maududi.
Maududi argued that there should be a complete separation between "church and state" (that is, between the orthodox ulema, in his view, and the state), and that Muslim societies should be purely dedicated to serving God. The divine state would be based on religious law, and people (even non-Muslims) were obligated to accept this authority if they were going to accept living in a Muslim society. In his view a Muslim was "an individual who is a Member of the House of Islam that stands for Freedom, Justice and the Rule of God". The existence of non-Muslims who, he said, can practice their beliefs in private, rests on an agreement (tanfidh) between the state and its inhabitants. They may enjoy full freedom, but must not create any objection to Islam. There should be a complete distinction between the public and the private.
Maududi felt that there could be no democracy in an Islamic state, as the Muslims of that state are bound to obey a divinely appointed law and Allah alone decides his law. In such a state even the shura (consultation) is not for administrative purposes but it is to consult with God's laws in Islamic Shari'at.[4] As a matter of principle, democracy contradicts a completely free state and constitutional government because democracy advocates the autonomy of the society from the state. It wants to destroy the absolute sovereignty of the prophet and of the Mujta-hid, which according to Maududi is also an essential principal of the Islamic ideology. He states in the introduction to his book What is Secularism?[5] In it Maududi states that secularism cannot mean anything but an impartial, even handed, justice and equality before law irrespective of race, class and colour.
Maududi viewed every worldly government as something to which non-Muslims could pay neither loyalty nor interest.
Maududi was a modern Islamist, not a traditionalist conservative.[6] He advocated changing the world and the human condition through Islam, and he dismissed the idea of a return to the golden age of Islam, which he felt had not existed in the seventh or even the thirteenth century.
Maududi's historical analysis suggests that the Muslim civilization entered its decline after the death of the second caliph, Umar. Since then, its claim to leadership was gradually displaced by the rising powers of Europe. Maududi saw the collapse of the Ottoman Empire as a result of the forces of secularism from within and the Crusades and "Ihrad" from without. He called for a return to Islam in education and to Islam as the law of the land, in order for Muslims to avoid further collapse. The "Muslims were not aware of the fact that their real problem was their own deviation from the principles of Islam, and that till they did not return to Islam, neither science nor technology, nor any other source of power could help them."[1]
Maududi was known for his extremely uncompromising stand on issues of Islam; he was an advocate of "no compromise in faith". Though, he spent much of his career as an armchair intellectual, this often took on much practical form in the fiery sermons which he delivered all over his country. He popularized the slogan "Dil Maanta Hai (Islam)" ("My heart is [with] Islam"). In one particular case he is said to have even written an ultimatum to the then leader of the Muslim League, Muhammad Ali Jinnah, demanding his acceptance of the Quran as the law of the land, or the partition of India would take place without him.[7]

\[
x^2 = 2x + 48
\]

First, we rearrange the equation to form a standard quadratic equation:

\[
x^2 - 2x - 48 = 0
\]

Next, we solve this quadratic equation using the quadratic formula:

\[
x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}

\[

\boxed{-6}

- The number divisible by 4 is: 4.

Chloroplasts are organelles found in plant and algal cells that are responsible for photosynthesis. They convert light energy into chemical energy in the form of glucose, which the plant uses for growth and other metabolic processes. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, a green pigment that absorbs light energy, and other pigments such as carotenoids and phycobilins that capture additional light energy. The chemical reaction that occurs inside the chloroplast is the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen through the process of photosynthesis.

The chloroplast has its own DNA, which is circular and separate from the nuclear DNA of the plant cell. The chloroplast DNA codes for a small number of proteins that are essential for the photosynthetic process. The majority of the proteins required for photosynthesis are encoded by the nuclear DNA and are imported into the chloroplast after the cell has been formed.

Chloroplasts have a double membrane structure. The outer membrane is permeable to small molecules, while the inner membrane is impermeable and separates the chloroplast's interior from the cytoplasm of the plant cell. The interior of the chloroplast is filled with a fluid called the stroma, which contains enzymes and other molecules involved in photosynthesis.

Within the chloroplast, there are numerous small structures called thylakoids. Thylakoids are arranged in stacks called grana, and they contain the photosynthetic pigments and enzymes necessary for photosynthesis. The pigments in thylakoids are arranged in units called reaction centers, which capture light energy and transfer it to other pigments in the photosystem. Photosystems are complexes of pigments and proteins that carry out the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.

The energy captured by photosystems is used to drive the synthesis of ATP and NADPH, which are used in the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis, also known as the Calvin cycle. In the Calvin cycle, carbon dioxide is fixed into organic compounds, such as glucose, and the energy from ATP and NADPH is used to power the synthesis of these compounds.

In summary, chloroplasts are essential organelles for photosynthesis and contain pigments and enzymes necessary for this process. The structure and function of chloroplasts are closely linked to the process of photosynthesis, which is responsible for producing the energy and organic compounds that plants and other photosynthetic organisms rely on for growth and survival.

Title: Oxygen Therapy in COVID-19 Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

Oxygen therapy, a critical component of management for patients with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), has been widely implemented to improve oxygenation levels and reduce mortality. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of various oxygen therapies in treating COVID-19 patients.

The authors conducted a comprehensive literature search through PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane Library databases, identifying 50 randomized controlled trials involving a total of 34,860 patients. The studies were divided into three categories based on the type of oxygen therapy used: room air, low-flow oxygen, and high-flow oxygen.

The results showed that patients receiving low-flow oxygen had a significantly lower risk of death compared to those given room air (OR = 0.56, 95% CI: 0.42-0.74). Furthermore, high-flow oxygen was associated with a reduced risk of mechanical ventilation (RR = 0.45, 95% CI: 0.34-0.60) and intensive care unit (ICU) admission (RR = 0.36, 95% CI: 0.28-0.46).

In summary, this meta-analysis suggests that oxygen therapy can be beneficial in the management of COVID-19 patients, with low-flow oxygen and high-flow oxygen showing significant advantages over room air in reducing mortality, the need for mechanical ventilation, and ICU admission.

Oxygen therapy has emerged as a vital treatment option for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients, significantly improving their quality of life and prognosis. This comprehensive review explores the latest evidence on oxygen therapy's efficacy, mechanisms of action, and potential complications.

The authors reviewed 70 clinical trials and observational studies published between 2015 and 2021, involving a total of 23,545 COPD patients. The studies examined various aspects of oxygen therapy, including long-term and short-term effects, delivery methods, and patient selection criteria.

Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) was found to reduce the risk of hospitalization due to respiratory exacerbations by 33% (95% CI: 0.67-0.75) and decrease the rate of all-cause mortality by 25% (95% CI: 0.56-0.63). Additionally, LTOT was associated with improved exercise tolerance, reduced fatigue, and enhanced cognitive function.

However, the review also highlighted the need for careful patient selection and monitoring to minimize the risks of oxygen toxicity, Volutrauma, and Paravolutrauma. These complications, though rare, can lead to serious health consequences, emphasizing the importance of individualized treatment plans.

In conclusion, oxygen therapy plays a pivotal role in managing COPD patients, offering substantial benefits when implemented judiciously. Future research should focus on optimizing patient selection criteria and improving the safety profile of oxygen therapy.

The foundation of any great coffee is the quality of the beans. I would select high-quality Arabica beans sourced from a region known for its excellent flavors, such as Colombia, Ethiopia, or Indonesia. Look for beans with a rich, well-balanced flavor profile that appeals to my taste preferences.

### Step 2: Freshness Is Key
To ensure the freshest coffee possible, I would purchase whole beans and grind them just before brewing. This minimizes oxidation and preserves the aromatic compounds that contribute to the coffee’s flavor.

### Step 3: Grind the Beans Properly
Using a burr grinder, I would grind the beans to the appropriate fineness for the brewing method I choose. For example:
- **Drip or Filter**: Medium-fine grind.
- **Espresso**: Fine grind.
- **Pour Over**: Medium grind.

### Step 4: Measure the Grounds
For a balanced cup, I would use a ratio of about 1:15 coffee to water. This translates to roughly 15 grams of grounds for every 240 milliliters of water. Measuring accurately ensures a consistent extraction and prevents over- or under-extraction.

Ensure all equipment is clean and preheated. This includes the coffee maker, brewer, and carafe to maintain optimal brewing temperature (around 92-96°C or 198-205°F).

Depending on the brewing method:
- **Drip/Filter**: Start the timer and let the water flow through.
- **Espresso**: Prepare the coffee and steam the milk for latte or cappuccino.
- **Pour Over**: Continue pouring water in a circular motion until all water has passed through the grounds.

Once brewing is complete, pour the coffee into preheated cups. Add any desired milk or creamer, sugar, or other condiments to enhance the flavor further. Serve immediately to fully appreciate the rich aroma and taste.

Lama

Lama is a Tibetan word meaning "superior one" or "great master". English-speakers commonly use the term Lama to refer to the ruling classes of Tibet. In traditional Buddhism there have been many types of lamas.
Ruler
The Tibetan Buddhist tradition, however, identifies three types of lama:
`Reincarnate lama
Vajra holder
Ngakpa`
Reincarnate lama or Tulku
The Tibetan word tülku (Wylie: sprul-sku) literally means "manifestation". Such lamas are considered to be manifestations of a teacher who has chosen - or been directed by a guru or deity - to reincarnate in order to continue his or her spiritual duties, such as leading a monastery or fulfilling a prophesied role within Buddhism. Lamas of this kind are believed to choose their own next incarnation when the time comes. Tulkus are always male.
There are many types of tulku:
Dharma tulku
This tulku is the reincarnation of a master of the teachings (Sanskrit: Dharma raja), who manifests himself for the sake of instructing sentient beings. There may be many monks of this type in a given monastery. Traditionally such a tulku would be the person who passes on the Tibetan lineage teaching in a monastery. In some cases, these lamas are called lama. Examples of some of these are 14th Dalai Lama, 10th Panchen Lama, Karmapa, Sakyong Mipham Rinpoche and Tarthang Tulku.
Spiritual tulku
These are tulkus who manifest themselves as the reincarnation of an accomplished spiritual master who has already given up his or her vajrayana vows. After the death of the old lama, the community of monks would assemble and select one of the candidates from among the candidates of potential reincarnation for the position of their teacher. After that, the lama would continue his duties to assist the community with spiritual teachings. Examples of these are Dudjom Rinpoche, the former Karmapa Choying Dorje.
Ordained tulku
Ordained tulkus manifest themselves to assume the great responsibilities of a teacher in the monastic tradition. Because of the voluminous aspects of the monastic tradition, it takes many years to master this system of practice and teaching. Once an ordained tulku has become completely qualified, he is asked to ordain another young boy who will be his successor and thus ensure the continuation of the teaching.
There are many non-ordained incarnate lamas also. Examples of this are Zayul Tertön, the former Taktshelpa Lama of Taktse Monastery in China, and the late Ligmincha Rinpoche.
The head of the Nyingma lineage of Tibetan Buddhism is known as a Ganden Tripa. The Karmapa, the Adhipati of the Karma Kagyu lineage, is chosen as the reincarnation of the former one. Until recently, the first incarnation was recognized by the leader of the school. Now the Tibetan government and the spiritual leader hold joint meetings to choose the reincarnation.
Vajra holder
Lama who's students are called tulkus.
Ngakpa
Ngakpa is Tibetan for "powerful man" or "victorious". A ngakpa is a tantric yogi, adept or practitioner in the Vajrayana, the form of Buddhism practiced in Tibet and other parts of Asia.
The term ngak means 'liberation' or 'bodhisattva' and the word ngakpa means 'liberator'. There is an equal category of ngakmama for nuns. A  ngakpa can be an ordained monk or layman, of either sex. Although no set of specific requirements exists for becoming a ngakpa, ngakpas must be adept in the Tibetan Buddhist tantra and must have received the necessary empowerments in this tradition.
The key differences in the use of the term ngakpa and lama include the historical and geographical distribution of the tradition of ngakpa in Tibet and the greater esoteric teachings and practices associated with the vajra holder (lama) vis a vis the ngakpa. At the Vajra Festival of Manasapan monastery in Kathmandu, Nepal, Khunga Lama, abbot of the monastery, referred to Vajra Pandita of Manasapan as ngakpa. Although Khunga Lama has had the privilege of studying with many of the teachers from the Kagyu schools, he was not raised in that environment nor was he specifically trained to teach this school. All ngakpas require some minimal instruction in the practice of samatha, the proper use of mantras and recitations, initiation by a higher ngakpa, and in physical yogas associated with Chakrasamvara and Hevajra. Many ngakpas are also great tantric meditators.
Ngakpa and ngakmama share many of the same titles and monastic codes as those shared by lamas and tulku.
Translated as Spiritual Teacher
A Rinpoche (literally: "precious one" or "He or She of special value") is a very common epithet applied to teachers or leaders in Tibetan Buddhism and some other Buddhist traditions. In a larger context the term rinpoche can be translated as "precious one." The term is an honorific epithet (e.g. head of an important monastery, etc.), title of nobility or venerated personage.
To be awarded the title, the one being honored usually has great spiritual ability and contributions, high moral standards, and is widely respected and honored. Particularly in former times, this title was given only to reincarnated lamas or tulkus or other high tantric masters of Vajrayana Buddhism. However, it is now common to refer to men and women who play important roles in the churches of Tibetan Buddhism as Rinpoche.

The Book of Kells (Irish: Codex Cenannensis[1] or Leabhar Cheannannais) is an illuminated manuscript of the four Gospels in Latin, created in about 800 by Celtic monks. The Gospels are attributed to four different authors: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. It is the most famous surviving Irish illuminated manuscript. The manuscript is also known as the病因 Dubh (literally, the black book) from its black purple goatskin cover. The original name of the manuscript was Cenániensis, from which the modern name "Kells" is derived. The book is so called because it was previously held in the Abbey of Kells, County Meath, where it is still shown to visitors. The surviving manuscript is kept at Trinity College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland.

### Background
The city of Kells (Cenn Fáelad in Irish) lies 53 km (33 mi) northwest of Dublin, near the River Boyne. Today the town comprises three villages. It is known as the home of the ancient manuscript.

Centuries later, the Book of Kells became the last thing to be moved from the Abbey of Kells before it was sacked by the Vikings around 841. The monks escaped with the manuscript and apparently took it back to Iona, a small island off Scotland's northwest coast, which was at the time the center of the Irish Church and a center of manuscript production. Iona's community may have been forced to flee the Viking attacks in the late 840s and were in turn pursued by the fierce King Alchred, who sent a fleet to the island of Iona and burned all of the manuscripts it held. The monks at Iona escaped into exile. Some travelled to Atha, west of Dublin, while others went to Kells, with the Book of Kells, probably arriving in 849.[10] Thus the manuscript was re-deposited in the Abbey of Kells, and at that time also became known as the Book of Kells.

Its combination of well-preserved art and lavish decoration make it among the most famous manuscripts in the world and one of Ireland's major tourist attractions.

### Manuscript
Illuminated manuscripts are rare for any age, and very few earlier Irish manuscripts have survived. The Book of Kells is considered the most elaborate example of Insular art (insular art is an amalgam of styles created in Ireland, Britain and parts of western Europe between the sixth and ninth centuries), and an early example of the Insular style that developed in Ireland during the Christianization of the region in the sixth century. The style is characterized by its interlacing figures (both geometric and naturalistic) and Celtic knot design. The combination of stylistic elements from Celtic, Anglo-Saxon and German art all in a single work of art gives it a unique quality. Later, as these styles grew apart, that combination of diverse stylistic elements could only be found in a few similar works.

Over the years, the manuscript has suffered damage from excessive handling, decay and fire (including one serious fire in the 1930s), has been rebound several times, and copies have been made; however, various restoration efforts were carried out to maintain and repair the work, to keep it in use, and to protect the original.
The Cenn Fáelad
The Cenn Fáelad or Cenániensis, the original title of the book, is derived from the fact that this manuscript was created in or near the town of Cenn Fáelad, now known as Kells, County Meath. This ancient Irish settlement lies about 53 kilometers north-west of Dublin city on the River Boyne and a short distance from the town of Drogheda.
The exact date of its creation is not known, but it is now generally believed to have been produced about 800, during the period of the Vikings' fierce invasion of Ireland. The Book of Kells is an illuminated manuscript which contains the four Gospels in Latin, prepared by Celtic monks. The dates suggested for its production are between 800 and 850 AD. There is, however, debate as to whether it was produced in a monastic house in Ireland or in Iona.
It is unclear exactly where the Book of Kells was created, though it was certainly crafted in an Irish monastery. The handwriting and style of illumination are similar to other well-known Insular manuscripts produced in either County Louth or County Dublin around 800, such as the Lindisfarne Gospels and the Eostre Gospels.[2] If it was made on the island of Iona it was probably taken to Ireland sometime in the 9th century when the monastery suffered attacks from the Vikings, perhaps from a monastery near Kells.

Refiner’s fire: How oil and gas companies are greening their energy production
Energy companies are harnessing the vast power of renewable energy to make fossil fuels greener
A tiny filament of yellow aluminum shows me the potential future of the fossil fuel industry.
The electrical material, no larger than a matchstick, generates heat when heated to more than 1,000 degrees Fahrenheit. It reacts with the air around it to burn brighter, providing a steady light. Then, after just a few seconds, it goes out, having emitted no smoke and released no carbon.
The material, manufactured at a 150-year-old steelworks in southwest England, gives an indication of just how powerful a catalyst renewable energy could be for the fossil fuel industry.
Moving away from fossil fuels would be beneficial for both the planet and companies, according to Jim Bentsen, COO of Advanced Metal Technologies (AMT), the business that produces the filament. “We do want people to eventually quit burning things,” he said. However, he added that “the world isn’t ready to quit burning things.”
Enter “refiner’s fire,” a sort of middle ground — and the angle of AMT’s business. The company produces a variety of materials that can absorb excess hydrogen produced during the refining process, allowing companies to continue using fossil fuels but decrease carbon emissions.
Other than our continued reliance on fossil fuels, the greatest irony about climate change is that energy companies that have powered the modern world for so long are also stepping up to the challenge of fixing our climate, much of it with the help of renewable energy. It’s part of a growing trend as the private energy industry realizes it can be both profitable and sustainable in the long run. The same goes for that filament that burns like a candle.
Renewable energy tech like solar and wind already represents about 3% of global power generation today, up from 0.1% in 1980, according to Ample, a solar power generation software company. That may sound like a modest increase, but it will likely accelerate in the coming years. For perspective, each year more capacity of renewable energy installations are added than all other energy types combined.
Renewable energy is more affordable than ever, and investment is growing, as the prospect of rapid climate change becomes increasingly clear. In January, 114 of the world’s leading financial institutions pledged to stop issuing any new financing for coal, the most polluting of the fossil fuels. There are signs that big energy companies are responding to the challenge, too. ExxonMobil, the world’s largest oil company, for instance, now projects that 36% of its reserves could be carbon-free by 2040, up from 25% last year, a sign that the company understands the changes that are coming, whether willingly or not.
Donna McClintock, an executive with BP, the world’s fifth largest oil company, told me that over the years, the focus of BP has slowly transitioned from simply extracting oil to manufacturing it.
“We have now moved to the point of manufacture of synthetic fuels with hydrogen,” she said, as well as other energy products derived from petroleum. “The emphasis has shifted away from just the extraction of oil.” In addition to an existing operation in India, BP has its sights set on using renewables to manufacture fuel in a U.S. plant that has been in the works for years.
For AMT’s Jim Bentsen, it was the rise of renewable energy that led him to his work with hydrogen and metals. Most of his business revolves around the filament, which is made up of nano-sized wires of titanium dioxide and aluminum, two metals that are known for their strong electrical properties.
Hydrogen is the fuel of the future, he says, and the filament helps energy companies utilize the abundant hydrogen byproduct of the oil refining process. It’s a game changer, he said, allowing companies to decarbonize their product and generate additional income streams from selling that hydrogen. With the filament, he adds, the entire refining process becomes greener, creating a steady stream of oxygen that creates a safer and cleaner environment for both humans and animals, all without relying on renewable energy.
The purpose of hydrogen isn’t just to enhance energy generation. It is more and more likely to be a component of other products. As an example, he pointed to several hydrogen-powered buses in operation in his hometown of Southampton.
“The hydrogen tanks are a problem,” he said. In order for the buses to be as green as possible, AMT’s filament is placed inside of the tanks, eliminating the need for a metal bladder inside that would otherwise require oil and aluminum to produce. Then, the buses have been placed into service on a ferry that serves the nearby Isle of Wight. There, they are used to transport approximately 100,000 passengers each year, releasing nothing but steam as they drive.
But how can we expect energy companies to make such a shift? It comes down to innovation and, at times, altruism, according to McClintock at BP. “They see the problems that are at hand,” she told me, “and the urgency to solve it.” Plus, the time to make the shift is now. The S&P Global E-Risk Forum found that on average, oil companies produce 40 million tons of CO2 emissions each year. “It’s a really significant problem,” McClintock says. “And it’s one that they recognize is significant.”
Refiner’s fire is no longer just a myth, but a tangible, real-world component of the energy production equation. As we work our way toward a more sustainable future, it’s becoming increasingly important for all energy companies to step up to the challenge.
